<script>
  // Restore the saved color scheme preference, or
  // enact the browser preference if "automatic",
  // without expecting DOM load to have completed.
  //
  // Also restore any saved readingmode and ToC display preferences.
  function initializeReadingPreferences() {
    let saved_theme = localStorage.getItem("ar5iv_theme") || "automatic";
    if (saved_theme === "automatic") {
      if (window.matchMedia("(prefers-color-scheme: dark)").matches) {
        saved_theme = "dark";
      }
    }
    if (saved_theme == "dark") {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "dark");
    } else {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "light");
    }

    const tocDisplay = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_toc_display');
    if (tocDisplay) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-toc-display", tocDisplay);
    }
    const readingMode = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_reading_mode');
    if (readingMode) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-reading-mode", readingMode);
    }
  }
  // Run as soon as JS starts, to minimize repainting
  initializeReadingPreferences();
</script>

  .arxiv-html-header { display: contents; }

  /* The paper controls' icons are blocks, so they sit centred (the pinned JS shows the theme
     icon by making its span a block). */
  .arxiv-html-site-chrome .ds-site-header-tools svg { display: block; width: 18px; height: 18px; flex-shrink: 0; fill: currentColor; }
  /* ar5iv dims every image in dark mode and puts it on a white wash, for paper figures;
     arXiv's own render as they are (the logo on the bar, the funder logos on their white
     chips). Important: ar5iv's dark rules are unlayered, as specific as
     :root:not([data-theme]) img:not(.ltx_no_dark_filter). */
  :is(.ds-site-header, .ds-site-footer) img { filter: none !important; }
  .ds-site-header img { background-color: transparent !important; }

  /* Wide (the theme's 1280px): the theme lays the body out as a grid whose full-width top rows
     were the band's and its sticky reader bar's. The band takes the first and scrolls away; the
     header, the paper's bar (no site navigation, the paper's controls), takes the second and
     stays in view, the one sticky bar, with the anchor clearance that requires (DESIGN-POLICIES).
     The controls show their names. */
  @media (min-width: 1280px) {
    html { scroll-padding-top: 80px; }
    .arxiv-html-site-chrome { display: contents; }
    .arxiv-html-site-chrome > #ds-announcement { grid-area: announce; }
    .arxiv-html-site-chrome > .ds-site-header { grid-area: header; position: sticky; top: 0; z-index: 3; }
    .arxiv-html-site-chrome .tool-icon { display: none; }
  }
  /* Narrow: the header scrolls away, and the controls show icons (names kept for screen
     readers; Why HTML? goes). The theme's contents panel is fixed below where its old sticky
     bar was, and hidden only once the reader has closed it, so until then it is an invisible box
     over the header and the paper: it shows only while open, under the chrome, in its place in
     the page. The paper's footer (build logs, reporting instructions) keeps the text's side
     inset; the theme gives it none, so it met the screen edges. */
  @media (max-width: 1279px) {
    .arxiv-html-site-chrome .tool-wide { display: none; }
    .arxiv-html-site-chrome .tool-label { position: absolute; width: 1px; height: 1px; overflow: hidden; clip: rect(0 0 0 0); white-space: nowrap; }
    html:not([data-toc-display="block"]) .ltx_page_navbar { display: none; }
    .ltx_page_navbar { position: absolute; top: auto; }
    .arxiv-html-footer { padding-inline: 1rem; }
  }

<article class="ltx_document ltx_authors_1line">
<h1 class="ltx_title ltx_title_document">Do Transformer World Models Give
<br class="ltx_break">Better Policy Gradients?</h1>
<div class="ltx_authors">
<span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Michel Ma
</span><span id="id1" class="ltx_note ltx_note_frontmatter ltx_thanks_contribution ltx_role_thanks"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">†</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">†</sup><span class="ltx_note_type">thanks: </span>Equal contribution.</span></span></span></span>
<span class="ltx_author_before">  </span><span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Tianwei Ni
</span></span>
<span class="ltx_author_before">  </span><span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">

</span></span>
<span class="ltx_author_before">  </span><span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Pierluca D’Oro<span id="footnotex1" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnotemark"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">1</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">1</sup><span class="ltx_note_type">footnotemark: </span>
          <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">1</span>



        </span></span></span>

<span class="ltx_author_before">  </span><span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">

</span><span class="ltx_author_notes"><span class="ltx_author_notes_content">
<span class="ltx_contact ltx_role_affiliation"><span class="ltx_contact_name">Affiliation: </span>Mila, Université de Montréal
</span>
<span class="ltx_contact ltx_role_affiliation"><span class="ltx_contact_name">Affiliation: </span><span id="id2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">{michel.ma, tianwei.ni, clement.gehring}@mila.quebec</span>
</span>
<span class="ltx_contact ltx_role_affiliation"><span class="ltx_contact_name">Affiliation: </span><span id="id3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">{pierluca.doro, pierre-luc.bacon}@mila.quebec</span>
</span></span></span></span></div>

<div id="abstract1" class="ltx_abstract"><h6 class="ltx_title ltx_title_abstract">Abstract</h6>

<p id="abstract1.1" class="ltx_p">A natural approach for reinforcement learning
is to predict future rewards by unrolling a
neural network world model, and to backpropagate through the resulting computational graph to learn a policy.
However, this method often becomes impractical for long horizons since typical world models induce hard-to-optimize loss landscapes.
Transformers are known to efficiently propagate gradients over long horizons: could they be the solution to this problem?
Surprisingly, we show that commonly-used transformer world models
produce <em id="abstract1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">circuitous gradient paths</em>, which can be detrimental to long-range policy gradients.
To tackle this challenge, we propose a class of world models called Actions World Models (AWMs), designed to provide more direct routes for gradient propagation. We integrate such AWMs into a policy gradient framework that underscores the relationship between network architectures and the policy gradient updates they inherently represent.
We demonstrate that AWMs can generate optimization landscapes that are easier to navigate even when compared to those from the simulator itself. This
property allows transformer AWMs to produce better policies than competitive baselines
in realistic long-horizon tasks.</p>

</div>
<div id="p1" class="ltx_para">
<table id="p1.1" class="ltx_tabular ltx_align_top">
<tbody class="ltx_tbody">
<tr id="p1.1.1" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="p1.1.1.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left"><span class="ltx_rule" style="width:0.0pt;height:24.0pt;--ltx-bg-color:black;display:inline-block;"></span></td></tr>
</tbody>
</table>
</div>
<section id="S1" class="ltx_section">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">1 </span>Introduction</h3>

<div id="S1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Given a class of parameterized policies, policy optimization methods aim to find parameters <math id="S1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\bm{\theta}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝜽</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\bm{\theta}}</annotation></semantics></math> that maximize a performance criterion <math id="S1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="J" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>J</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">J</annotation></semantics></math> – typically the expected sum of rewards over the episodes of experiences generated by an agent in an environment.
When the environment dynamics are known and differentiable, the gradient of the objective <math id="S1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="J" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>J</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">J</annotation></semantics></math> can be directly evaluated through automatic differentiation and used
to optimize <math id="S1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="J" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>J</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">J</annotation></semantics></math> by gradient ascent.
If the dynamics are unknown, a differentiable world model can be trained on interaction data, whose predicted states will be backpropagated through.
This model-based approach to reinforcement learning (RL) has been explored early on in the field with <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib52" title="" class="ltx_ref">Werbos (1974)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib44" title="" class="ltx_ref">Schmidhuber (1990)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib34" title="" class="ltx_ref">Miller et al. (1995)</a></cite> and led to contemporary work in deep RL such as <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hafner et al. (2022)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hafner et al. (2023)</a></cite>.
While backpropagation through time <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib51" title="" class="ltx_ref">Werbos (1990)</a></cite> using a world model is conceptually appealing and readily compatible with deep learning practice, most attempts to scale it up have been unsuccessful beyond a few dozen steps <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hafner et al. (2022)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ghugare et al. (2023)</a></cite>.
Indeed, even in the presence of perfectly accurate differentiable simulators, policy gradients obtained by backpropagation through time can quickly become unstable over long horizons <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib49" title="" class="ltx_ref">Suh et al. (2022)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib32" title="" class="ltx_ref">Metz et al. (2021)</a></cite>.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S1.F1" class="ltx_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_3">
<figure id="S1.F1.sf1" class="ltx_figure ltx_figure_panel ltx_align_center"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2402.05290v2/markovian-diagram.svg" id="S1.F1.sf1.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:181/103;" width="181" height="103"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">(a) </span>Markovian world model.</figcaption>
</figure></div><div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_3">
<figure id="S1.F1.sf2" class="ltx_figure ltx_figure_panel ltx_align_center"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2402.05290v2/history-diagram.svg" id="S1.F1.sf2.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:181/104;" width="181" height="104"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">(b) </span>History World Model.</figcaption>
</figure></div><div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_3">
<figure id="S1.F1.sf3" class="ltx_figure ltx_figure_panel ltx_align_center"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2402.05290v2/awm-diagram.svg" id="S1.F1.sf3.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:181/103;" width="181" height="103"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">(c) </span>Actions World Model.</figcaption>
</figure></div></div>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 1: </span><span id="S1.F1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Diagram illustrating gradient flows through different world model types from states to actions.</span> Circuitous (longer than necessary) gradient paths go through connections highlighted in red. An Actions World Model has no circuitous gradient paths, allowing gradients to directly flow from states to actions through a single application of a world model.</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">This problem of stability in differentiating through world models over long horizons echoes similar challenges observed in sequence modeling. The latter field has experienced numerous advances in deep network architectures specifically aimed at alleviating this challenge.
As a notable example, attention-based models such as transformers were designed to directly propagate gradients from any output to any input arbitrarily far in the past, within their context length <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib45" title="" class="ltx_ref">Schmidhuber (1992)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib50" title="" class="ltx_ref">Vaswani et al. (2017)</a></cite>.
It is, therefore, natural to ponder whether using a transformer as a world model and differentiating through it could overcome the difficulties encountered in model-based policy optimization.
Or, in other words, to ask the question: <em id="S1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">do transformer world models give better policy gradients?</em> In this paper, we provide a new answer to this question: surprisingly, transformers do not necessarily confer the same benefit for policy optimization when used as world models conditioned on the full history of states and actions. Instead, conditioning solely on a sequence of actions tends to yield better-behaved policy gradients. This, in turn, leads to improved temporal credit assignment and policy performance.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">We first show that backpropagating naively through a transformer predicting the next state conditioned on the full history
 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib33" title="" class="ltx_ref">Micheli et al. (2022)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chen et al. (2022)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib42" title="" class="ltx_ref">Robine et al. (2023)</a></cite> does not necessarily lead to better policy gradients in long-horizon tasks.
We demonstrate, conceptually and theoretically, that this phenomenon can be attributed to the existence of <em id="S1.p3.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">circuitous gradient paths</em>: long state-to-state gradient paths generated during the autoregressive unrolling of the model (see Figure <a href="#S1.F1" title="Figure 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ Do Transformer World Models Give Better Policy Gradients?" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>).</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">To avoid the creation of those longer-than-necessary gradient paths,
we propose an alternative class of world models, which we call <em id="S1.p4.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">Actions World Models</em> (AWMs), of the form <math id="S1.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\hat{s}_{t+1}=g(s_{1},a_{1},\dots,a_{t-1},a_{t})}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>s</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>g</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\hat{s}_{t+1}=g(s_{1},a_{1},\dots,a_{t-1},a_{t})}</annotation></semantics></math> conditioned solely on the history of past actions and an initial state.
An AWM is forced to create its own internal dynamics, potentially very different from the one of the environment, while being able to predict future states. This inductive bias constrains the temporal accumulation of gradients to only happen within the neural network of the AWM,
fully harnessing its gradient properties.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p5" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p5.1" class="ltx_p">We show theoretically that an AWM directly inherits the gradient propagation properties of the underlying network architecture.
Thus, AWMs yield policy gradients subject to bounds similar to the ones previously derived in deep sequence models <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib38" title="" class="ltx_ref">Pascanu et al. (2013b)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kerg et al. (2020)</a></cite>.
Additionally, our theoretical framework provides a unified perspective on many backpropagation-based policy optimization methods by exposing the relationship between the network architecture and the policy gradient updates that they induce.
For instance, it allows us to cast backpropagation through unrolled Markovian dynamics <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">Heess et al. (2015)</a></cite> as a specific AWM instantiated with a vanilla recurrent neural network. Our framework paves the way for new algorithmic developments by fostering novel synergies between the study of network architectures in deep learning and the policy optimization updates they implicitly express.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p6" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p6.1" class="ltx_p">Finally, through a series of experiments, we showcase the remarkable empirical properties of backpropagation-based policy optimization with AWMs.
We demonstrate in illustrative domains with chaotic or non-differentiable dynamics that AWMs can give better policy gradients than the simulator itself, by forcing the policy optimization landscape to be easy to optimize. This leads to successful policy optimization via backpropagation even when the same procedure would fail with the true underlying model.
On a testbed of realistic long-horizon tasks <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">Howe et al. (2022)</a></cite>, we benchmark policy optimization with transformer AWMs against other competitive model-free and model-based methods, showing superior performance.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2" class="ltx_section">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">2 </span>Background</h3>

<div id="S2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Problem definition</span>  We are interested in deterministic<span id="footnote1" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">1</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">1</sup>
            <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">1</span>



          See <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib28" title="" class="ltx_ref">Laidlaw et al. (2023)</a></cite> for a discussion on the importance of the study of deterministic MDPs.</span></span></span> discrete-time finite-horizon Markov Decision Processes (MDPs) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">Fairbank, 2014</a>)</cite>, defined as <math id="S2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{M}=(\mathcal{S},\mathcal{A},f,r,H,s_{1})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℳ</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒮</mi><mo>,</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒜</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>f</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>r</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>H</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{M}=(\mathcal{S},\mathcal{A},f,r,H,s_{1})</annotation></semantics></math>, where <math id="S2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{S}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{n}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒮</mi><mo>⊆</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mi>n</mi></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{S}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{n}</annotation></semantics></math> is the state space, <math id="S2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{A}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{m}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒜</mi><mo>⊆</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mi>m</mi></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{A}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{m}</annotation></semantics></math> is the action space, <math id="S2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="f:\mathcal{S}\times\mathcal{A}\to\mathcal{S}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mrow><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒮</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒜</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒮</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f:\mathcal{S}\times\mathcal{A}\to\mathcal{S}</annotation></semantics></math> is the differentiable transition dynamics, <math id="S2.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r:\mathcal{S}\to\mathbb{R}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒮</mi><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mi>ℝ</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r:\mathcal{S}\to\mathbb{R}</annotation></semantics></math> is the known differentiable reward function, <math id="S2.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="H" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>H</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">H</annotation></semantics></math> is the horizon and <math id="S2.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s_{1}\in\mathcal{S}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>s</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>∈</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒮</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s_{1}\in\mathcal{S}</annotation></semantics></math> is the initial state.
The behavior of an agent in the environment is described by a policy <math id="S2.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi_{{\bm{\theta}}}:\mathcal{S}\to\mathcal{A}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>π</mi><mi>𝜽</mi></msub><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒮</mi><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒜</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi_{{\bm{\theta}}}:\mathcal{S}\to\mathcal{A}</annotation></semantics></math>, belonging to a space of parameterized differentiable deterministic<span id="footnote2" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">2</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">2</sup>
            <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">2</span>



          This assumption can be relaxed to a stochastic policy using the reparameterization trick <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib27" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kingma &amp; Welling, 2014</a>)</cite>.</span></span></span> stationary Markov policies <math id="S2.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Pi=\{\pi_{{\bm{\theta}}}:{\bm{\theta}}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Π</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msub><mi>π</mi><mi>𝜽</mi></msub><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mrow><mi>𝜽</mi><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mi>d</mi></msup></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Pi=\{\pi_{{\bm{\theta}}}:{\bm{\theta}}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}\}</annotation></semantics></math>.
For clarity, we focus on stationary rewards and dynamics, but our results could readily be adapted to the non-stationary case.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Backpropagation-based Policy Optimization</span> The goal of the agent is to maximize the cumulative episodic rewards. In the rest of the paper, we consider the following problem:</p>
<table id="S2.E1" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S2.E1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\begin{gathered}\begin{aligned} \text{maximize}\quad&amp;J^{f}({\bm{\theta}};H):=\sum_{t=1}^{H}r(s_{t}),&amp;\text{subject to}\quad&amp;s_{t+1}=f(s_{t},a_{t}),\,a_{k}=\pi_{\bm{\theta}}(\text{sg}[s_{k}])\kern 5.0pt.\end{aligned}\end{gathered}" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mtable displaystyle="true"><mtr><mtd><mtable columnspacing="0pt" displaystyle="true"><mtr><mtd class="ltx_align_right" columnalign="right"><mtext>maximize</mtext></mtd><mtd class="ltx_align_left" columnalign="left"><mrow><mrow><mrow><msup><mi>J</mi><mi>f</mi></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝜽</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>H</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="0.111em">:=</mo><mrow><munderover><mo movablelimits="false">∑</mo><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>H</mi></munderover><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow></mtd><mtd class="ltx_align_right" columnalign="right"><mtext>subject to</mtext></mtd><mtd class="ltx_align_left" columnalign="left"><mrow><mi>s</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>a</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo rspace="0.337em">,</mo><mi>a</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mi>k</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>π</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mi>𝜽</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mtext>sg</mtext><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mi>s</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mi>k</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">]</mo><mo rspace="0.222em" stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>.</mo></mrow></mtd></mtr></mtable></mtd></mtr></mtable><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\begin{gathered}\begin{aligned} \text{maximize}\quad&amp;J^{f}({\bm{\theta}};H):=\sum_{t=1}^{H}r(s_{t}),&amp;\text{subject to}\quad&amp;s_{t+1}=f(s_{t},a_{t}),\,a_{k}=\pi_{\bm{\theta}}(\text{sg}[s_{k}])\kern 5.0pt.\end{aligned}\end{gathered}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(1)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S2.p2.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathrm{sg}[\cdot]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>sg</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">⋅</mo><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathrm{sg}[\cdot]</annotation></semantics></math> is the stop-gradient operator.
Model-based policy gradient methods solve this problem by unrolling (simulating) the dynamics forward and computing the gradient of the corresponding unconstrained problem. The presence of the stop gradient operator in our formulation aligns with the contemporary practice <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hafner et al., 2022</a>; <a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hafner et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ghugare et al., 2023</a>)</cite>. Its inclusion in our formulation does not impact
performance (see Appendix <a href="#A6.SS1" title="F.1 Ablation on Stop Gradient ‣ Appendix F Myriad Environments ‣ Appendix ‣ Do Transformer World Models Give Better Policy Gradients?" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">F.1</span></a> for an ablation) and simplifies our theoretical analysis.</p>
</div>

</div>
</div>
</figure>
<div id="S2.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">When the true dynamics <math id="S2.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="f" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>f</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f</annotation></semantics></math> are unknown,
a transition function <math id="S2.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{f}_{\bm{\psi}}(s_{t},a_{t})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>𝝍</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{f}_{\bm{\psi}}(s_{t},a_{t})</annotation></semantics></math> belonging to a space of parameterized differentiable functions <math id="S2.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{F}=\{f_{\bm{\psi}}:{\bm{\psi}}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\psi}}\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℱ</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msub><mi>f</mi><mi>𝝍</mi></msub><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mrow><mi>𝝍</mi><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>ψ</mi></msub></msup></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{F}=\{f_{\bm{\psi}}:{\bm{\psi}}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\psi}}\}</annotation></semantics></math> must be learned to perform policy optimization.
Given transitions <math id="S2.p3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s_{t},a_{t},s_{t+1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s_{t},a_{t},s_{t+1}</annotation></semantics></math> sampled from the environment, an approximate Markovian world model <math id="S2.p3.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{f}_{\bm{\psi}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>𝝍</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{f}_{\bm{\psi}}</annotation></semantics></math> can be learned with the loss <math id="S2.p3.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\ell^{\hat{f}}(\tau;{\bm{\psi}})=\sum_{t=1}^{H-1}\|s_{t+1}^{\tau}-\hat{f}_{\bm{\psi}}(s_{t}^{\tau},a_{t}^{\tau})\|^{2}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msup><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>^</mo></mover></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>τ</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>𝝍</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="0.111em">=</mo><mrow><msubsup><mo rspace="0em">∑</mo><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>H</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msubsup><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><mrow><msubsup><mi>s</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>τ</mi></msubsup><mo>−</mo><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>𝝍</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mi>s</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>τ</mi></msubsup><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mi>a</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>τ</mi></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\ell^{\hat{f}}(\tau;{\bm{\psi}})=\sum_{t=1}^{H-1}\|s_{t+1}^{\tau}-\hat{f}_{\bm{\psi}}(s_{t}^{\tau},a_{t}^{\tau})\|^{2}}</annotation></semantics></math>,
where <math id="S2.p3.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\tau=(s_{1}^{\tau},a_{1}^{\tau},\dots,s_{H}^{\tau})}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>τ</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mi>s</mi><mn>1</mn><mi>τ</mi></msubsup><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mi>a</mi><mn>1</mn><mi>τ</mi></msubsup><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mi>s</mi><mi>H</mi><mi>τ</mi></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\tau=(s_{1}^{\tau},a_{1}^{\tau},\dots,s_{H}^{\tau})}</annotation></semantics></math> is a trajectory. For the remainder of this paper, consider <math id="S2.p3.m8" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="\|\bullet\|" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo rspace="0em">∥</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">∙</mo><mo lspace="0em">∥</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\|\bullet\|</annotation></semantics></math> to denote the <math id="S2.p3.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="L^{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>L</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">L^{2}</annotation></semantics></math> norm.
Given a learned model, policy and initial state, the corresponding return <math id="S2.p3.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="J^{\hat{f}}({\bm{\theta}};{\bm{\psi}})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>J</mi><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>^</mo></mover></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝜽</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>𝝍</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">J^{\hat{f}}({\bm{\theta}};{\bm{\psi}})</annotation></semantics></math> can be computed through rollouts and the gradient <math id="S2.p3.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\nabla_{{\bm{\theta}}}J^{\hat{f}}({\bm{\theta}};{\bm{\psi}})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mo>∇</mo><mi>𝜽</mi></msub><msup><mi>J</mi><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>^</mo></mover></msup></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝜽</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>𝝍</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\nabla_{{\bm{\theta}}}J^{\hat{f}}({\bm{\theta}};{\bm{\psi}})</annotation></semantics></math> can be obtained by backpropagation.
We call this basic algorithm, outlined in Algorithm <a href="#alg1" title="In 2 Background ‣ Do Transformer World Models Give Better Policy Gradients?" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>, <em id="S2.p3.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">Backpropagation-based Policy Optimization</em> (BPO).</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3" class="ltx_section">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">3 </span>Policy Gradient Computation with History World Models</h3>

<div id="S3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">When running Algorithm <a href="#alg1" title="In 2 Background ‣ Do Transformer World Models Give Better Policy Gradients?" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>, the performance of the resulting policy depends on the quality of the gradient approximation.
Effective long-term credit assignment capabilities are required for computing the gradient <math id="S3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\nabla_{a_{t}}r(s_{t+k})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mo>∇</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></msub><mi>r</mi></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\nabla_{a_{t}}r(s_{t+k})</annotation></semantics></math>, as provided by the world model, for potentially very large values of <math id="S3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math> in challenging control tasks. This means understanding how a reward at a temporally distant time changes in response to variations in a specific action taken at an earlier moment.
Therefore, the long-term credit assignment properties of a model-based policy optimization algorithm are intimately tied to the structure of the unrolled world model.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">One fundamental fact about backpropagation is that its success in learning long-term dependencies is intimately linked to the length of the paths involved in the neural network’s gradient computation <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib37" title="" class="ltx_ref">Pascanu et al., 2013a</a>; <a href="#bib.bib55" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhang et al., 2016</a>)</cite>.
Indeed, the success of transformers is often attributed to this phenomenon: “one key factor affecting the ability to learn such dependencies is the length of the paths forward and backward signals have to traverse in the network” <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib50" title="" class="ltx_ref">Vaswani et al., 2017</a>)</cite>.
When trained for sequence modeling tasks, transformers stand out compared to other architectures because the length of these paths does not linearly increase with the sequence length.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Recent model-based RL approaches have introduced the use of transformer History World Models (HWMs), which predict the next state as <math id="S3.p3.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="\hat{s}_{t}=h(s_{1:{t-1}},a_{1:{t-1}})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>s</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>h</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{s}_{t}=h(s_{1:{t-1}},a_{1:{t-1}})</annotation></semantics></math> based on the full history of states and actions  <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib33" title="" class="ltx_ref">Micheli et al., 2022</a>; <a href="#bib.bib42" title="" class="ltx_ref">Robine et al., 2023</a>)</cite>. Their use leads to improved performance due to better prediction abilities but, surprisingly, these approaches were not able to take advantage of the gradient propagation properties of the transformer architecture, as exemplified by previous work which only unrolls them for a few steps <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chen et al., 2022</a>)</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.p4.1" class="ltx_p">In practice, an HWM is unrolled in this manner to compute the cumulative reward for a given policy:</p>
<table id="S3.E2" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\begin{gathered}\begin{aligned} \text{maximize}\quad&amp;J^{h}({\bm{\theta}};H):=\sum_{t=1}^{H}r(\hat{s}_{t}),&amp;\text{subject to}\quad&amp;\hat{s}_{t+1}=h(\hat{s}_{1:t},a_{1:k}),\,a_{k}=\pi_{\bm{\theta}}(\text{sg}[\hat{s}_{k}])\kern 5.0pt.\end{aligned}\end{gathered}" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mtable movablelimits="false">∑</mo><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>H</mi></munderover><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>s</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow></mtd><mtd class="ltx_align_right" columnalign="right"><mtext>subject to</mtext></mtd><mtd class="ltx_align_left" columnalign="left"><mrow><mover rspace="0.337em">,</mo><mi>a</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mi>k</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>π</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mi>𝜽</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mtext>sg</mtext><mo \text{maximize}\quad&amp;J^{h}({\bm{\theta}};H):=\sum_{t=1}^{H}r(\hat{s}_{t}),&amp;\text{subject to}\quad&amp;\hat{s}_{t+1}=h(\hat{s}_{1:t},a_{1:k}),\,a_{k}=\pi_{\bm{\theta}}(\text{sg}[\hat{s}_{k}])\kern 5.0pt.\end{aligned}\end{gathered}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(2)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div>
<div id="S3.p5" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.p5.1" class="ltx_p">HWMs are typically learned by employing a prediction objective <math id="S3.p5.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="\ell^{h}(\tau;{\bm{\psi}})=\sum_{t=1}^{H-1}\|s_{t+1}^{\tau}-h_{\bm{\psi}}(s_{1:t}^{\tau},a_{1:t}^{\tau})\|^{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mi>h</mi></msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>τ</mi><mo>;</mo><mi>𝝍</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo rspace="0.111em">=</mo><msubsup><mo rspace="0em">∑</mo><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>H</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msubsup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0.167em">∥</mo><msubsup><mi>s</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>τ</mi></msubsup><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>h</mi><mi>𝝍</mi></msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mi>s</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow><mi>τ</mi></msubsup><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mi>a</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow><mi>τ</mi></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><msup><mo lspace="0em">∥</mo><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\ell^{h}(\tau;{\bm{\psi}})=\sum_{t=1}^{H-1}\|s_{t+1}^{\tau}-h_{\bm{\psi}}(s_{1:t}^{\tau},a_{1:t}^{\tau})\|^{2}</annotation></semantics></math>, similar to the one employed for a Markovian model,
where <math id="S3.p5.m2" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="s_{1:t}^{\tau}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>s</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><msup><mrow></mrow><mi>τ</mi></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s_{1:t}^{\tau}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S3.p5.m3" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="a_{1:t}^{\tau}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>a</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><msup><mrow></mrow><mi>τ</mi></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a_{1:t}^{\tau}</annotation></semantics></math> denote subsequences of states and actions from an episode <math id="S3.p5.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tau" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>τ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau</annotation></semantics></math>.
While history-conditioned dynamics are in principle not necessary in an MDP<span id="footnote3" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">3</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">3</sup>
            <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">3</span>



          Policy gradients can be computed through equation <a href="#S3.E2" title="In 3 Policy Gradient Computation with History World Models ‣ Do Transformer World Models Give Better Policy Gradients?" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a> similarly in partially observable MDPs (POMDP), where states are replaced with observations. The resulting analysis would, therefore, still hold in a POMDP.</span></span></span>, one may hope that the gradient properties of transformers might manifest themselves positively in the policy gradient. It stands to reason that the policy gradients through a transformer may be able to more effectively capture long-term dependencies than a Markovian model would.
Nonetheless, this apparently natural usage of a transformer has unintended consequences for policy optimization.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.p6" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.p6.1" class="ltx_p">Visually, we show in Figure <a href="#S1.F1" title="Figure 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ Do Transformer World Models Give Better Policy Gradients?" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a> the gradient paths induced by unrolling a <em id="S3.p6.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">state-based</em> world model, whether Markovian (Figure <a href="#S1.F1.sf1" title="In Figure 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ Do Transformer World Models Give Better Policy Gradients?" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1a</span></a>) or history-dependent (Figure <a href="#S1.F1.sf2" title="In Figure 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ Do Transformer World Models Give Better Policy Gradients?" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1b</span></a>), from state predictions to actions. The impact of an action on a future state is measured by navigating the paths connecting the two generated by a world model. Some of these are <em id="S3.p6.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">circuitous gradient paths</em>:
these paths do not go from state to action directly but instead include auto-regressive state predictions from the model itself.
Such paths are perilous for long-horizon policy optimization; errors, noise, and gradient behaviors that may be good internally can rapidly degrade outside the model, reducing the possible advantages of backpropagating through transformers.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.p7" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.p7.1" class="ltx_p">In particular, the following theorem shows that even if the gradient of a transformer HWM is bounded, the resulting policy gradient can still grow exponentially. The proof of this and the rest of our results can be found in Appendix <a href="#A1" title="Appendix A Proofs ‣ Appendix ‣ Do Transformer World Models Give Better Policy Gradients?" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">A</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<div id="Thmtheorem1" class="ltx_theorem ltx_theorem_theorem">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_runin ltx_title_theorem"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_theorem"><span id="Thmtheorem1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Theorem 1</span></span><span id="Thmtheorem1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">.</span></h6>
<div id="Thmtheorem1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Thmtheorem1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="Thmtheorem1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Let the gradient norm of <math id="Thmtheorem1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="h" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>h</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">h</annotation></semantics></math> with respect to its inputs be bounded by <math id="Thmtheorem1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="L_{a}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>L</mi><mi>a</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">L_{a}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="Thmtheorem1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="L_{s}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>L</mi><mi>s</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">L_{s}</annotation></semantics></math>: <math id="Thmtheorem1.p1.m4" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="\|\frac{\partial h(\hat{s}_{1:t},a_{1:t})}{\partial a_{k}}\|\leq L_{a}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo rspace="0.167em">∥</mo><mfrac><mrow><mo>∂</mo><mi>h</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mover stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mo>∂</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>k</mi></msub></mrow></mfrac><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0.0835em">∥</mo><mo lspace="0.0835em">≤</mo><mi>L</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mi>a</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\|\frac{\partial h(\hat{s}_{1:t},a_{1:t})}{\partial a_{k}}\|\leq L_{a}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="Thmtheorem1.p1.m5" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="\|\frac{\partial h(\hat{s}_{1:t},a_{1:t})}{\partial\hat{s}_{i}}\|\leq L_{s}" display="inline" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>a</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mo>∂</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>s</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></mfrac><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0.0835em">∥</mo><mo lspace="0.0835em">≤</mo><mi>L</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mi>s</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\|\frac{\partial h(\hat{s}_{1:t},a_{1:t})}{\partial\hat{s}_{i}}\|\leq L_{s}</annotation></semantics></math> for all <math id="Thmtheorem1.p1.m6" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="s_{1:t},a_{1:t},k,i" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>s</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>a</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>k</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s_{1:t},a_{1:t},k,i</annotation></semantics></math>. Let <math id="Thmtheorem1.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>r</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r</annotation></semantics></math> be the <math id="Thmtheorem1.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="L_{r}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>L</mi><mi>r</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">L_{r}</annotation></semantics></math>-Lipschitz reward function from a Markov Decision Process <math id="Thmtheorem1.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{M}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℳ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{M}</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="Thmtheorem1.p1.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Pi_{\bm{\theta}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">Π</mi><mi>𝛉</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Pi_{\bm{\theta}}</annotation></semantics></math> a parametric space of differentiable deterministic <math id="Thmtheorem1.p1.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="L_{\pi}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>L</mi><mi>π</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">L_{\pi}</annotation></semantics></math>-policies. Given <math id="Thmtheorem1.p1.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi_{\bm{\theta}}\in\Pi_{\bm{\theta}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>π</mi><mi>𝛉</mi></msub><mo>∈</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">Π</mi><mi>𝛉</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi_{\bm{\theta}}\in\Pi_{\bm{\theta}}</annotation></semantics></math>, the norm of the policy gradient <math id="Thmtheorem1.p1.m13" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\nabla_{\bm{\theta}}J^{h}({\bm{\theta}};H)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mo>∇</mo><mi>𝛉</mi></msub><msup><mi>J</mi><mi>h</mi></msup></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝛉</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>H</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\nabla_{\bm{\theta}}J^{h}({\bm{\theta}};H)</annotation></semantics></math> of <math id="Thmtheorem1.p1.m14" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi_{\bm{\theta}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>π</mi><mi>𝛉</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi_{\bm{\theta}}</annotation></semantics></math> under a History World Model <math id="Thmtheorem1.p1.m15" class="ltx_Math" alttext="h" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>h</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">h</annotation></semantics></math> grows asymptotically as a function of the horizon <math id="Thmtheorem1.p1.m16" class="ltx_Math" alttext="H" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>H</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">H</annotation></semantics></math> as:</span></p>
<table id="S3.EGx1" class="ltx_equationgroup ltx_eqn_align ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody id="S3.Ex1"><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S3.Ex1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle\|\nabla_{\theta}J^{h}({\bm{\theta}};H)\|" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><mrow><mrow><msub><mo rspace="0.167em">∇</mo><mi>θ</mi></msub><msup><mi>J</mi><mi>h</mi></msup></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝜽</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>H</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle\|\nabla_{\theta}J^{h}({\bm{\theta}};H)\|</annotation></semantics></math></td>

</table>
</div>
</div>
<figure id="S3.F2" class="ltx_figure ltx_align_floatright" style="width:39%;"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2402.05290v2/double-pend-rl.svg" id="S3.F2.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:209/149;" width="209" height="149"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 2: </span><span id="S3.F2.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Transformer AWMs outperforms all BPO baselines in chaotic environments.</span> Final performances of BPO with different world models on the double-pendulum environment (10 seeds <math id="S3.F2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pm" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>±</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pm</annotation></semantics></math> std).</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S3.p8" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.p8.1" class="ltx_p">The exponential dependency, related to exploding gradients in RNNs, is apparent in Figure <a href="#S1.F1.sf2" title="In Figure 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ Do Transformer World Models Give Better Policy Gradients?" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1b</span></a>, where the longest path from any given state to action is no shorter than the longest path through a Markovian model. The bound is shown to be tight in Appendix <a href="#A1.SS1" title="A.1 Tightness of Theorem ‣ Appendix A Proofs ‣ Appendix ‣ Do Transformer World Models Give Better Policy Gradients?" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">A.1</span></a>. In the one-dimensional case, when all gradients are positive scalars, the above bound can be turned into a lower bound.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.p9" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.p9.1" class="ltx_p">To illustrate the negative effects of circuitous gradient paths in practice, we conduct experiments in a double-pendulum environment where the agent must move the double-pendulum to a target position. We describe and visualize the task more precisely in Section <a href="#S5" title="5 Experiments ‣ Do Transformer World Models Give Better Policy Gradients?" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a>.
The results in Figure <a href="#S3.F2" title="Figure 2 ‣ 3 Policy Gradient Computation with History World Models ‣ Do Transformer World Models Give Better Policy Gradients?" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a> show that BPO does not lead to successful policies with both Markovian models and HWMs in this notoriously chaotic environment.
This result demonstrates that state-conditioned transformers do not provide any benefits to policy gradients due to circuitous gradient paths, unlike in the traditional supervised learning setting where they were initially introduced.
In the rest of the paper, we will see how using transformers as a different type of world model allows us not only to overcome the limitations of Markovian models and HWMs, but also to outperform policy optimization performed by differentiating through the dynamics of the simulator, as well as competitive model-free approaches.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4" class="ltx_section">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">4 </span>Policy Gradient Computation with Actions World Models</h3>

<div id="S4.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Policy gradients obtained from state-based world models, whether Markovian models or HWMs, are necessarily computed by backpropagating through sequences of states generated by autoregressively unrolling the models. Each state prediction uses as input previously generated states; consequently, the longest path between any action and reward traverses through circuitous gradient paths in the state space, <em id="S4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">regardless of the underlying world model architecture</em>. Through careful examination of Figure <a href="#S1.F1" title="Figure 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ Do Transformer World Models Give Better Policy Gradients?" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a> and Theorem <a href="#Thmtheorem1" title="Theorem 1. ‣ 3 Policy Gradient Computation with History World Models ‣ Do Transformer World Models Give Better Policy Gradients?" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>, it quickly becomes apparent that the state dependency in <math id="S4.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="h" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>h</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">h</annotation></semantics></math> or <math id="S4.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="f" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>f</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f</annotation></semantics></math> is at the root cause of such paths.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Inspired by this observation, we propose to remove all circuitous gradient paths in the simplest and most direct way: conditioning the world model on actions only. We thus consider a model which predicts a future state given an initial state and a sequence of actions. The resulting model, which we call an <em id="S4.p2.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">Actions World Model</em> (AWM), is of the form <math id="S4.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{s}_{t+1}=g(s_{1},a_{1},a_{2},\ldots,a_{t})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>s</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>g</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{s}_{t+1}=g(s_{1},a_{1},a_{2},\ldots,a_{t})</annotation></semantics></math>.
This structure for the world model constrains gradients to pass directly from rewards to actions through the network parameterizing the AWM. Note that previous work showed that actions are theoretically sufficient to predict future states in deterministic MDPs and often sufficient in practice for most stochastic environments <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib41" title="" class="ltx_ref">Rezende et al., 2020</a>)</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Given an AWM, a policy is learned by computing and employing (as in Algorithm <a href="#alg1" title="In 2 Background ‣ Do Transformer World Models Give Better Policy Gradients?" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>) the gradient of the objective:</p>
<table id="S4.E3" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S4.E3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\begin{gathered}\begin{aligned}
