5.0pt.\end{aligned}\end{gathered}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(3)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S4.p3.2" class="ltx_p">An AWM can be trained in a similar manner to a Markovian model or an HWM, by using the loss <math id="S4.p3.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="{\ell^{g}(\tau;{\bm{\psi}})=\sum_{t=1}^{H-1}\|s_{t+1}^{\tau}-g_{\bm{\psi}}(s_{1},a_{1:t}^{\tau})\|^{2}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mi>g</mi></msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>τ</mi><mo>;</mo><mi>𝝍</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo rspace="0.111em">=</mo><msubsup><mo rspace="0em">∑</mo><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>H</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msubsup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0.167em">∥</mo><msubsup><mi>s</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>τ</mi></msubsup><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>g</mi><mi>𝝍</mi></msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mi>a</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow><mi>τ</mi></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><msup><mo lspace="0em">∥</mo><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\ell^{g}(\tau;{\bm{\psi}})=\sum_{t=1}^{H-1}\|s_{t+1}^{\tau}-g_{\bm{\psi}}(s_{1},a_{1:t}^{\tau})\|^{2}}</annotation></semantics></math>,
computed likewise using states from an episode <math id="S4.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tau" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>τ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.p4.1" class="ltx_p">We will now show that, despite the seemingly counter-intuitive removal of state inputs, AWMs naturally connect the theory of policy gradients and sequence modeling with neural networks and provide a framework in which transformers can give high-quality policy gradients.</p>
</div>
<section id="S4.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.1 </span>Markovian Models are RNN Actions World Models</h4>

<div id="S4.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The intuition that policy gradients computed through an unrolled Markovian model prescribed by equation <a href="#S2.E1" title="In 2 Background ‣ Do Transformer World Models Give Better Policy Gradients?" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a> resembles the process of backpropagating through a recurrent neural network has been pointed out in multiple prior works <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">Heess et al. (2015)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib32" title="" class="ltx_ref">Metz et al. (2021)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib49" title="" class="ltx_ref">Suh et al. (2022)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib56" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhang et al. (2023)</a></cite>. Yet, a formal account of this relationship has never been shown.
Via the framework provided by AWMs, the next proposition shows how recurrent neural networks and policy gradients are connected, offering a first glimpse at the connection between neural network architectures, AWMs and policy gradient computation in MDPs.</p>
</div>
<div id="Thmproposition1" class="ltx_theorem ltx_theorem_proposition">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_runin ltx_title_theorem"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_theorem"><span id="Thmproposition1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Proposition 1</span></span><span id="Thmproposition1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">.</span></h6>
<div id="Thmproposition1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Thmproposition1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="Thmproposition1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Let
<math id="Thmproposition1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="f\text{-}\texttt{RNN}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mtext class="ltx_mathvariant_italic">-</mtext><mtext class="ltx_mathvariant_monospace">RNN</mtext></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f\text{-}\texttt{RNN}</annotation></semantics></math>
be a recurrent network with its recurrent cell being the dynamics <math id="Thmproposition1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="f" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>f</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f</annotation></semantics></math> of the MDP <math id="Thmproposition1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{M}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℳ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{M}</annotation></semantics></math>, and <math id="Thmproposition1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="g_{f\text{-}\texttt{RNN}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>g</mi><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mtext class="ltx_mathvariant_italic">-</mtext><mtext class="ltx_mathvariant_monospace">RNN</mtext></mrow></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">g_{f\text{-}\texttt{RNN}}</annotation></semantics></math> denote an AWM instantiated with <math id="Thmproposition1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="f\text{-}\texttt{RNN}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mtext class="ltx_mathvariant_italic">-</mtext><mtext class="ltx_mathvariant_monospace">RNN</mtext></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f\text{-}\texttt{RNN}</annotation></semantics></math>. Then,</span></p>
<table id="S4.EGx2" class="ltx_equationgroup ltx_eqn_align ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody id="S4.Ex2"><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S4.Ex2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle\nabla_{\bm{\theta}}J^{g_{f\text{-}\texttt{RNN}}}({\bm{\theta}};H)=\nabla_{\bm{\theta}}J^{f}({\bm{\theta}};H)." display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mrow><msub><mo>∇</mo><mi>𝜽</mi></msub><msup><mi>J</mi><msub><mi>g</mi><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mtext class="ltx_mathvariant_italic">-</mtext><mtext class="ltx_mathvariant_monospace">RNN</mtext></mrow></mrow></msub></msup></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝜽</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>H</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><msub><mo rspace="0.167em">∇</mo><mi>𝜽</mi></msub><msup><mi>J</mi><mi>f</mi></msup></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝜽</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>H</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle\nabla_{\bm{\theta}}J^{g_{f\text{-}\texttt{RNN}}}({\bm{\theta}};H)=\nabla_{\bm{\theta}}J^{f}({\bm{\theta}};H).</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">The above proposition tells us that the policy gradient computed through a Markovian model is, in fact, equivalent to the one computed through an AWM when instantiating <math id="S4.SS1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="g" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>g</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">g</annotation></semantics></math> as a recurrent neural network with a specific recurrent cell. Crucially, this not only provides grounding for gradient estimation with AWMs but also solidifies a fundamental fact that will be analyzed in-depth in this section: policy gradient computation by differentiating through unrolled Markovian models can be understood to be fundamentally ill-behaved due to its correspondence to an RNN structure.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.2 </span>Theoretical Properties of Actions World Models</h4>

<div id="S4.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Through the concept of Actions World Models, we have established a direct connection between deep sequence models and policy gradient computation. We will now exploit this connection to characterize the asymptotic behavior of the policy gradient depending on the underlying neural network architecture employed as an AWM. To do so, we leverage the following theorem.</p>
</div>
<div id="Thmtheorem2" class="ltx_theorem ltx_theorem_theorem">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_runin ltx_title_theorem"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_theorem"><span id="Thmtheorem2.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Theorem 2</span></span><span id="Thmtheorem2.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">.</span></h6>
<div id="Thmtheorem2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Thmtheorem2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="Thmtheorem2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Let <math id="Thmtheorem2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="r" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>r</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">r</annotation></semantics></math> be the <math id="Thmtheorem2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="L_{r}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>L</mi><mi>r</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">L_{r}</annotation></semantics></math>-Lipschitz reward function from a Markov Decision Process <math id="Thmtheorem2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{M}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℳ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{M}</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="Thmtheorem2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Pi_{\bm{\theta}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">Π</mi><mi>𝛉</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Pi_{\bm{\theta}}</annotation></semantics></math> a parametric space of differentiable deterministic <math id="Thmtheorem2.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="L_{\pi}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>L</mi><mi>π</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">L_{\pi}</annotation></semantics></math>-policies. Given <math id="Thmtheorem2.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi_{\bm{\theta}}\in\Pi_{\bm{\theta}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>π</mi><mi>𝛉</mi></msub><mo>∈</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">Π</mi><mi>𝛉</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi_{\bm{\theta}}\in\Pi_{\bm{\theta}}</annotation></semantics></math>, the norm of the policy gradient <math id="Thmtheorem2.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\nabla_{\bm{\theta}}J^{g}({\bm{\theta}};H)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mo>∇</mo><mi>𝛉</mi></msub><msup><mi>J</mi><mi>g</mi></msup></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝛉</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>H</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\nabla_{\bm{\theta}}J^{g}({\bm{\theta}};H)</annotation></semantics></math> of <math id="Thmtheorem2.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi_{\bm{\theta}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>π</mi><mi>𝛉</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi_{\bm{\theta}}</annotation></semantics></math> under an action world model <math id="Thmtheorem2.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="g" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>g</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">g</annotation></semantics></math> as a function of the horizon <math id="Thmtheorem2.p1.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="H" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>H</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">H</annotation></semantics></math> can upper bounded as:</span></p>
<table id="S4.EGx3" class="ltx_equationgroup ltx_eqn_align ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody id="S4.Ex3"><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S4.Ex3.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="\displaystyle\left\|\nabla_{\bm{\theta}}J^{g}({\bm{\theta}};H)\right\|\leq L_{r}L_{\pi}\sum_{t=1}^{H}\sum_{k=1}^{t-1}\left\|\frac{\partial g(s_{1},a_{1:t-1})}{\partial a_{k}}\right\|." display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mo>‖</mo><msub><mo rspace="0.167em">∇</mo><mi>𝜽</mi></msub><msup><mi>J</mi><mi>g</mi></msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝜽</mi><mo>;</mo><mi>H</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>‖</mo></mrow><mo>≤</mo><msub><mi>L</mi><mi>r</mi></msub><msub><mi>L</mi><mi>π</mi></msub><mstyle displaystyle="true"><munderover><mo movablelimits="false">∑</mo><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>H</mi></munderover></mstyle><mstyle displaystyle="true"><munderover><mo movablelimits="false">∑</mo><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></munderover></mstyle><mrow><mo>‖</mo><mstyle displaystyle="true"><mfrac><mrow><mo>∂</mo><mi>g</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>a</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mo>∂</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>k</mi></msub></mrow></mfrac></mstyle><mo>‖</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle\left\|\nabla_{\bm{\theta}}J^{g}({\bm{\theta}};H)\right\|\leq L_{r}L_{\pi}\sum_{t=1}^{H}\sum_{k=1}^{t-1}\left\|\frac{\partial g(s_{1},a_{1:t-1})}{\partial a_{k}}\right\|.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">This theorem holds for any differentiable AWM <math id="S4.SS2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="g" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>g</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">g</annotation></semantics></math>, and establishes a worst-case relationship between the Jacobian of the AWM w.r.t. its inputs (i.e., actions) and the policy gradient.
Notably, the result implies that the policy gradient does not explode if the Jacobian of the AWM does not explode. In contrast, this may not be true even for well-behaved HWM.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">We will now leverage the generality of the previous result to characterize the asymptotic behavior of the policy gradient computed using different neural network architectures for an AWM. First, let us consider an AWM instantiated with a simple recurrent neural network:</p>
<table id="S4.EGx4" class="ltx_equationgroup ltx_eqn_align ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody id="S4.E4"><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S4.E4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle\text{(}g_{\texttt{RNN}}\text{)}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mtext>(</mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>g</mi><mtext class="ltx_mathvariant_monospace">RNN</mtext></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mtext>)</mtext></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle\text{(}g_{\texttt{RNN}}\text{)}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_eqn_cell"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S4.E4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle x_{t+1}=\sigma(W_{x}x_{t})+W_{a}a_{t}+b;" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>σ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>W</mi><mi>x</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><msub><mi>W</mi><mi>a</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi></mrow></mrow><mo>;</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle x_{t+1}=\sigma(W_{x}x_{t})+W_{a}a_{t}+b;</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_eqn_cell"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_eqn_cell"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S4.E4.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle\hat{s}_{t+1}=W_{o}x_{t+1}," display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>s</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>W</mi><mi>o</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle\hat{s}_{t+1}=W_{o}x_{t+1},</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(4)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S4.SS2.p3.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S4.SS2.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sigma" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>σ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sigma</annotation></semantics></math> is an activation function with gradient norm bounded by <math id="S4.SS2.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\left\|diag(\sigma^{\prime}(x))\right\|\leq\frac{1}{\beta}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mo>‖</mo><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>a</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>g</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msup><mi>σ</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>‖</mo></mrow><mo>≤</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mi>β</mi></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\left\|diag(\sigma^{\prime}(x))\right\|\leq\frac{1}{\beta}</annotation></semantics></math> for some constant <math id="S4.SS2.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\beta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>β</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\beta</annotation></semantics></math>.
Then, the following result holds.</p>
</div>
<div id="Thmtheorem2.Thmcorollary1" class="ltx_theorem ltx_theorem_corollary">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_runin ltx_title_theorem"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_theorem"><span id="Thmtheorem2.Thmcorollary1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Corollary 2.1</span></span><span id="Thmtheorem2.Thmcorollary1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">.</span></h6>
<div id="Thmtheorem2.Thmcorollary1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Thmtheorem2.Thmcorollary1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="Thmtheorem2.Thmcorollary1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Let <math id="Thmtheorem2.Thmcorollary1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="g_{\texttt{RNN}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>g</mi><mtext class="ltx_mathvariant_monospace">RNN</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">g_{\texttt{RNN}}</annotation></semantics></math> be an Actions World Model instantiated with a recurrent neural network as in Equation <a href="#S4.E4" title="In 4.2 Theoretical Properties of Actions World Models ‣ 4 Policy Gradient Computation with Actions World Models ‣ Do Transformer World Models Give Better Policy Gradients?" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a> and <math id="Thmtheorem2.Thmcorollary1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\eta=\|W_{x}^{T}\|\frac{1}{\beta}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>η</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><msubsup><mi>W</mi><mi>x</mi><mi>T</mi></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mi>β</mi></mfrac></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\eta=\|W_{x}^{T}\|\frac{1}{\beta}</annotation></semantics></math>. The asymptotic behavior of the norm of the policy gradient <math id="Thmtheorem2.Thmcorollary1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\nabla_{\bm{\theta}}J^{g_{\texttt{RNN}}}({\bm{\theta}};H)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mo>∇</mo><mi>𝛉</mi></msub><msup><mi>J</mi><msub><mi>g</mi><mtext class="ltx_mathvariant_monospace">RNN</mtext></msub></msup></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝛉</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>H</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\nabla_{\bm{\theta}}J^{g_{\texttt{RNN}}}({\bm{\theta}};H)</annotation></semantics></math> as a function of the horizon H can be described as:</span></p>
<table id="S4.EGx5" class="ltx_equationgroup ltx_eqn_align ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody id="S4.Ex4"><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S4.Ex4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle\left\|\nabla_{{\bm{\theta}}}J^{g_{\texttt{RNN}}}({\bm{\theta}};H)\right\|=O\left(\eta^{H}\right)." display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mo>‖</mo><mrow><mrow><msub><mo rspace="0.167em">∇</mo><mi>𝜽</mi></msub><msup><mi>J</mi><msub><mi>g</mi><mtext class="ltx_mathvariant_monospace">RNN</mtext></msub></msup></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝜽</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>H</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>‖</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>O</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><msup><mi>η</mi><mi>H</mi></msup><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle\left\|\nabla_{{\bm{\theta}}}J^{g_{\texttt{RNN}}}({\bm{\theta}};H)\right\|=O\left(\eta^{H}\right).</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS2.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Corollary <a href="#S4.EGx5" title="Corollary 2.1. ‣ 4.2 Theoretical Properties of Actions World Models ‣ 4 Policy Gradient Computation with Actions World Models ‣ Do Transformer World Models Give Better Policy Gradients?" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2.1</span></a> shows that, in the worst case, the policy gradient computed with an AWM instantiated with an RNN backbone can explode exponentially fast with respect to the problem horizon if the spectral radius of <math id="S4.SS2.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W_{x}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>W</mi><mi>x</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W_{x}</annotation></semantics></math> exceeds <math id="S4.SS2.p4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\beta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>β</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\beta</annotation></semantics></math>. Just like Theorem <a href="#Thmtheorem1" title="Theorem 1. ‣ 3 Policy Gradient Computation with History World Models ‣ Do Transformer World Models Give Better Policy Gradients?" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>, the above bound can be written as a lower bound when all gradients are positive scalars, therefore it is tight.
This result will allow us to compare the gradient provided by an RNN AWM with the one provided by a transformer AWM, but it is also connected with gradient computation with Markovian models: as seen in Proposition <a href="#S4.EGx2" title="Proposition 1. ‣ 4.1 Markovian Models are RNN Actions World Models ‣ 4 Policy Gradient Computation with Actions World Models ‣ Do Transformer World Models Give Better Policy Gradients?" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>, using a Markovian model to compute the policy gradient, either given or learned, implies an RNN-structure for the AWM.
Theorem <a href="#S4.EGx5" title="Corollary 2.1. ‣ 4.2 Theoretical Properties of Actions World Models ‣ 4 Policy Gradient Computation with Actions World Models ‣ Do Transformer World Models Give Better Policy Gradients?" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2.1</span></a> is a consequence of foundational theory of RNNs <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">Bengio et al., 1994</a>; <a href="#bib.bib38" title="" class="ltx_ref">Pascanu et al., 2013b</a>)</cite>, thus formalizing the intuition that the recurrent nature of policy gradients through Markovian models make both exploiting differentiable simulators <math id="S4.SS2.p4.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="f" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>f</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f</annotation></semantics></math> and learned models <math id="S4.SS2.p4.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{f}_{\bm{\psi}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>𝝍</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{f}_{\bm{\psi}}</annotation></semantics></math> difficult <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib32" title="" class="ltx_ref">Metz et al., 2021</a>; <a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">Heess et al., 2015</a>)</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.p5" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS2.p5.1" class="ltx_p">Let us now apply Theorem <a href="#Thmtheorem2" title="Theorem 2. ‣ 4.2 Theoretical Properties of Actions World Models ‣ 4 Policy Gradient Computation with Actions World Models ‣ Do Transformer World Models Give Better Policy Gradients?" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a> to a layer of self-attention AWM <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib50" title="" class="ltx_ref">Vaswani et al., 2017</a>)</cite>. Given <math id="S4.SS2.p5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="Q\in\mathbb{R}^{1\times d_{z}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>Q</mi><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>z</mi></msub></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">Q\in\mathbb{R}^{1\times d_{z}}</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S4.SS2.p5.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d_{z}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>z</mi></msub></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d_{z}}</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S4.SS2.p5.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="V\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d_{o}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>V</mi><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>o</mi></msub></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">V\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d_{o}}</annotation></semantics></math>, we define <math id="S4.SS2.p5.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\text{Attention}(Q,K,V):=\text{softmax}(QK^{T})V" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mtext>Attention</mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>Q</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>K</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>V</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>:=</mo><mrow><mtext>softmax</mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>Q</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>K</mi><mi>T</mi></msup></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>V</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\text{Attention}(Q,K,V):=\text{softmax}(QK^{T})V</annotation></semantics></math>. Using a set of weight matrices, a self-attention AWM predicts the next state as follows<span id="footnote4" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">4</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">4</sup>
              <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">4</span>



            Without loss of generality, the dependency on the initial state is not included in the self-attention layer.</span></span></span>:</p>
<table id="S4.EGx6" class="ltx_equationgroup ltx_eqn_align ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody id="S4.E5"><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S4.E5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle\text{(}g_{\texttt{ATT}}\text{)}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mtext>(</mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>g</mi><mtext class="ltx_mathvariant_monospace">ATT</mtext></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mtext>)</mtext></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle\text{(}g_{\texttt{ATT}}\text{)}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_eqn_cell"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S4.E5.m2" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="\displaystyle\hat{s}_{t+1}=\text{Attention}(a_{t}W_{q}^{T},a_{1:t}W_{k}^{T},a_{1:t}W_{v}^{T})\kern 5.0pt." display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>s</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mtext>Attention</mtext><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><msubsup><mi>W</mi><mi>q</mi><mi>T</mi></msubsup><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><msubsup><mi>W</mi><mi>k</mi><mi>T</mi></msubsup><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><msubsup><mi>W</mi><mi>v</mi><mi>T</mi></msubsup><mo rspace="0.222em" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle\hat{s}_{t+1}=\text{Attention}(a_{t}W_{q}^{T},a_{1:t}W_{k}^{T},a_{1:t}W_{v}^{T})\kern 5.0pt.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_eqn_cell"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(5)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S4.SS2.p5.2" class="ltx_p">We can now characterize the behavior of the policy gradient computed with a self-attention AWM.</p>
</div>
<div id="Thmtheorem2.Thmcorollary2" class="ltx_theorem ltx_theorem_corollary">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_runin ltx_title_theorem"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_theorem"><span id="Thmtheorem2.Thmcorollary2.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Corollary 2.2</span></span><span id="Thmtheorem2.Thmcorollary2.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">.</span></h6>
<div id="Thmtheorem2.Thmcorollary2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Thmtheorem2.Thmcorollary2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="Thmtheorem2.Thmcorollary2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Let <math id="Thmtheorem2.Thmcorollary2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="g_{\texttt{ATT}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>g</mi><mtext class="ltx_mathvariant_monospace">ATT</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">g_{\texttt{ATT}}</annotation></semantics></math> be an attention-based Actions World Model instantiated with self-attention as in equation <a href="#S4.E5" title="In 4.2 Theoretical Properties of Actions World Models ‣ 4 Policy Gradient Computation with Actions World Models ‣ Do Transformer World Models Give Better Policy Gradients?" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a>.
The asymptotic behavior of the norm of the policy gradient <math id="Thmtheorem2.Thmcorollary2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\nabla_{{\bm{\theta}}}J^{g_{\texttt{ATT}}}({\bm{\theta}};H)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mo>∇</mo><mi>𝛉</mi></msub><msup><mi>J</mi><msub><mi>g</mi><mtext class="ltx_mathvariant_monospace">ATT</mtext></msub></msup></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝛉</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>H</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\nabla_{{\bm{\theta}}}J^{g_{\texttt{ATT}}}({\bm{\theta}};H)</annotation></semantics></math> as a function of the horizon <math id="Thmtheorem2.Thmcorollary2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="H" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>H</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">H</annotation></semantics></math> can be described as:</span></p>
<table id="S4.EGx7" class="ltx_equationgroup ltx_eqn_align ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody id="S4.Ex5"><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S4.Ex5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle\left\|\nabla_{{\bm{\theta}}}J^{g_{\texttt{ATT}}}({\bm{\theta}};H)\right\|=O\left(H^{3}\right)." display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mo>‖</mo><mrow><mrow><msub><mo rspace="0.167em">∇</mo><mi>𝜽</mi></msub><msup><mi>J</mi><msub><mi>g</mi><mtext class="ltx_mathvariant_monospace">ATT</mtext></msub></msup></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝜽</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>H</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>‖</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>O</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><msup><mi>H</mi><mn>3</mn></msup><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle\left\|\nabla_{{\bm{\theta}}}J^{g_{\texttt{ATT}}}({\bm{\theta}};H)\right\|=O\left(H^{3}\right).</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.p6" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS2.p6.1" class="ltx_p">This result shows that the norm of the policy gradient computed through a self-attention AWM has a worst-case polynomial dependency on the horizon instead of an exponential one shown in Theorem <a href="#Thmtheorem1" title="Theorem 1. ‣ 3 Policy Gradient Computation with History World Models ‣ Do Transformer World Models Give Better Policy Gradients?" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a> and Corollary <a href="#S4.EGx5" title="Corollary 2.1. ‣ 4.2 Theoretical Properties of Actions World Models ‣ 4 Policy Gradient Computation with Actions World Models ‣ Do Transformer World Models Give Better Policy Gradients?" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2.1</span></a>. Since the output of a transformer model only depends on the sequence length through the attention mechanism, this characterization captures the gradient dynamics of the transformer model itself. It shows that, by eliminating all circuitous gradient paths, AWMs provide a framework for transformers to translate their favorable gradient properties towards better policy gradients, unlike state-conditioned models.</p>
</div>

</figure></div><div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_3">
<figure id="S4.F3.sf2" class="ltx_figure ltx_figure_panel ltx_align_center"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2402.05290v2/discontinuous_trajectory.svg" id="S4.F3.sf2.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:146/110;" width="146" height="110"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">(b) </span>Example trajectory with non-differentiable point at <math id="S4.F3.sf2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t\approx 0.25" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>≈</mo><mn>0.25</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t\approx 0.25</annotation></semantics></math>.</figcaption>
</figure></div><div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_3">
<figure id="S4.F3.sf3" class="ltx_figure ltx_figure_panel ltx_align_center"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2402.05290v2/discontinuous_landscape.svg" id="S4.F3.sf3.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:163/110;" width="163" height="110"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">(c) </span>Final return with respect to the initial action for different models.</figcaption>
</figure></div></div>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 3: </span><span id="S4.F3.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">AWMs ignore non-differentiable points in the state space.</span> (a) After the block is pushed with some initial action, it bounces off the wall, instantaneously reversing its velocity. (b) Visualization of the point of non-differentiability in the state space. (c) Learning a Markovian model or a HWM causes catastrophic compounding errors, but an AWM can still accurately model the final reward when varying the initial action. Learned dynamics are trained offline on a dataset collected using random actions. </figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S5" class="ltx_section">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">5 </span>Experiments</h3>

<div id="S5.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Backpropagation through Actions World Models produces policy gradients with no circuitous gradient paths. Consequently, the longest gradient path from an action to any reward strictly depends on the AWM internals, while the path through state-based world models scales with the horizon, regardless of the model architecture. This section empirically explores how this phenomenon benefits the policy optimization process (see Appendix <a href="#A3" title="Appendix C Reinforcement Learning Hyperparameters ‣ Appendix ‣ Do Transformer World Models Give Better Policy Gradients?" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">C</span></a> for hyperparameters of all experiments).</p>
</div>
<section id="S5.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">5.1 </span>Empirical Properties of Action World Models</h4>

<div id="S5.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">By removing the need to explicitly model the state dynamics auto-regressively, AWMs can internally build a more appropriate world model for policy optimization. Using environments inspired by real-world physical systems, we highlight two particular properties of AWMs: skipping points of complex state-space dynamics and smoothing out ill-behaved policy optimization landscapes.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.SS1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">AWMs overcome non-differentiable dynamics</span>  Unlike state-based world models, AWMs directly map actions to future states without explicitly predicting intermediate states. This mapping allows AWMs to skip points of potentially complex dynamics in the state space, which are not always necessary for policy optimization. For example, consider points of non-differentiability (e.g., contact points) in real-world systems (e.g., physical systems). These points make directly using the simulator dynamics for BPO impossible and can cause catastrophic compounding errors for state-conditioned world models. However, these points often exist even if the dependency of rewards on actions is smooth and well-behaved everywhere. In such cases, AWMs can be used to side-step the non-differentiability of the state dynamics. To illustrate this point, we examine a <em id="S5.SS1.p2.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">one-bounce</em> environment, shown in Figure <a href="#S4.F3" title="Figure 3 ‣ 4.2 Theoretical Properties of Actions World Models ‣ 4 Policy Gradient Computation with Actions World Models ‣ Do Transformer World Models Give Better Policy Gradients?" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>. In this task, an agent must push a block towards a wall with some initial action, such that the block bounces off the wall and ends up at some predetermined goal state after <math id="S5.SS1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="H" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>H</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">H</annotation></semantics></math> steps. A single terminal reward is given at <math id="S5.SS1.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t=H" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>H</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t=H</annotation></semantics></math> measuring the distance of the block to the goal state. Even though the state trajectory is non-differentiable due to the wall bounce, the final state of the block is actually well-behaved with respect to initial actions (Figure <a href="#S4.F3.sf2" title="In Figure 3 ‣ 4.2 Theoretical Properties of Actions World Models ‣ 4 Policy Gradient Computation with Actions World Models ‣ Do Transformer World Models Give Better Policy Gradients?" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3b</span></a> and Figure <a href="#S4.F3.sf3" title="In Figure 3 ‣ 4.2 Theoretical Properties of Actions World Models ‣ 4 Policy Gradient Computation with Actions World Models ‣ Do Transformer World Models Give Better Policy Gradients?" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3c</span></a>). Consequently, we show in Figure <a href="#S4.F3.sf3" title="In Figure 3 ‣ 4.2 Theoretical Properties of Actions World Models ‣ 4 Policy Gradient Computation with Actions World Models ‣ Do Transformer World Models Give Better Policy Gradients?" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3c</span></a>
that AWMs can accurately predict the final reward while an unrolled Markovian or HWM cannot. Notably, the resulting AWM thus allows to easily use backpropagation-based policy optimization even in the presence of an underlying non-differentiable environment dynamics.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.SS1.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">AWMs overcome chaotic dynamics</span>  
In many real-world systems (e.g., robots), the chaotic dynamics of an environment can create a remarkably complex mapping from actions to rewards over time or a highly non-smooth return landscape <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib40" title="" class="ltx_ref">Rahn et al., 2023</a>)</cite>.
In such systems, even when a differentiable simulator is available, it gives ill-behaved gradients and generates an optimization landscape that is hard to navigate <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib49" title="" class="ltx_ref">Suh et al., 2022</a>)</cite>.
We now show that transformer AWMs are able to take full advantage of the inductive biases of the underlying neural networks, naturally generating policy optimization landscapes that are easy to navigate. This happens regardless of the complexity of the real dynamics while preserving the global problem structure and allowing good policies to be found more easily.
To demonstrate this, we use a prototypical chaotic system, a double-pendulum task depicted in Figure <a href="#S5.F4.sf1" title="In Figure 4 ‣ 5.1 Empirical Properties of Action World Models ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ Do Transformer World Models Give Better Policy Gradients?" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4a</span></a>.
In this environment, the agent’s initial action determines the initial angular position of the inner pendulum. Afterwards, the system is rolled out for <math id="S5.SS1.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="H" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>H</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">H</annotation></semantics></math> steps. The objective is to get the pendulums to be in some predefined goal state after <math id="S5.SS1.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="H" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>H</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">H</annotation></semantics></math> steps. A terminal reward is given measuring the distance between the final observed state and the desired goal state. We illustrate in Figure <a href="#S5.F4.sf2" title="In Figure 4 ‣ 5.1 Empirical Properties of Action World Models ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ Do Transformer World Models Give Better Policy Gradients?" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4b</span></a> and Figure <a href="#S5.F4.sf3" title="In Figure 4 ‣ 5.1 Empirical Properties of Action World Models ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ Do Transformer World Models Give Better Policy Gradients?" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4c</span></a> the chaotic nature of the task, showing respectively that the norm of the true gradient of the return with respect to the initial action grows exponentially with the episode length <math id="S5.SS1.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="H" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>H</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">H</annotation></semantics></math>, and that the true return landscape is extremely difficult to navigate for long horizons.
Figure <a href="#S5.F4.sf2" title="In Figure 4 ‣ 5.1 Empirical Properties of Action World Models ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ Do Transformer World Models Give Better Policy Gradients?" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4b</span></a> shows that transformers provide stable gradients when used as AWMs, while the gradient provided by HWMs explodes similarly to the true gradients.
AWMs generate a smooth and accurate approximation of the return landscape (Figure <a href="#S5.F4.sf3" title="In Figure 4 ‣ 5.1 Empirical Properties of Action World Models ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ Do Transformer World Models Give Better Policy Gradients?" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4c</span></a>), which gradient ascent can easily navigate, leading to better policies when used for backpropagation-based policy optimization compared to all the other world models (Figure <a href="#S3.F2" title="Figure 2 ‣ 3 Policy Gradient Computation with History World Models ‣ Do Transformer World Models Give Better Policy Gradients?" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>).</p>
</div>
<figure id="S5.F4" class="ltx_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_3">
<figure id="S5.F4.sf1" class="ltx_figure ltx_figure_panel ltx_align_center"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2402.05290v2/double_pend_vis.svg" id="S5.F4.sf1.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_img_portrait" style="aspect-ratio:50/91;" width="50" height="91"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">(a) </span>Double-pendulum.</figcaption>
</figure></div><div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_3">
<figure id="S5.F4.sf2" class="ltx_figure ltx_figure_panel ltx_align_center"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2402.05290v2/double-pend-grads.svg" id="S5.F4.sf2.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:127/87;" width="127" height="87"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">(b) </span>Gradient norms.</figcaption>
</figure></div><div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_3">
<figure id="S5.F4.sf3" class="ltx_figure ltx_figure_panel ltx_align_center"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2402.05290v2/double-pend-return-landscape.svg" id="S5.F4.sf3.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:372/87;" width="372" height="87"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">(c) </span>Final returns with respect to the initial action for different models when <math id="S5.F4.sf3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="H=100" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>H</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>100</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">H=100</annotation></semantics></math>.
</figcaption>
</figure></div></div>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 4: </span><span id="S5.F4.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Transformer AWMs smooths out chaotic dynamics.</span> (a) A double-pendulum environment where an initial position must be chosen in order to achieve some pre-determined goal state after <math id="S5.F4.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="H" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>H</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">H</annotation></semantics></math> steps. Different transition models are learned on a data set of random trajectories. (b) The mean gradient norm of the final state with respect to the initial action for each model is computed over 50 different random actions for different horizons. (c) Final return according to different models with respect to different initial actions for <math id="S5.F4.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="H=100" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>H</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>100</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">H=100</annotation></semantics></math>.</figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">5.2 </span>Benchmarking Credit Assignment with AWMs</h4>

<div id="S5.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We now show that transformers employed as AWMs can give better policies in environments which require long-horizon planning. We focus on eight tasks from the Myriad testbed <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">Howe et al. (2022)</a></cite>. Myriad provides continuous MDPs inspired by real-world problems <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib29" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lenhart &amp; Workman (2007)</a></cite> with configurable horizons. In Myriad, the agent requires better temporal credit assignment capabilities to solve problems with longer episode lengths, in contrast to other RL benchmarks (e.g., focused on simple robotics locomotion), which typically feature a short effective horizon <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib28" title="" class="ltx_ref">Laidlaw et al. (2023)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib36" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ni et al. (2023)</a></cite> regardless of the episode length.
Additional information about Myriad and its experiments are provided in Appendix <a href="#A6" title="Appendix F Myriad Environments ‣ Appendix ‣ Do Transformer World Models Give Better Policy Gradients?" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">F</span></a>. All aggregate results use the IQM <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">Agarwal et al. (2021)</a></cite>.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S5.F5" class="ltx_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_2">
<figure id="S5.F5.sf1" class="ltx_figure ltx_figure_panel ltx_align_center"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2402.05290v2/aggregate_iqm.svg" id="S5.F5.sf1.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:214/153;" width="214" height="153"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">(a) </span>Final performances of BPO for different horizons.</figcaption>
</figure></div><div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_2">
<figure id="S5.F5.sf2" class="ltx_figure ltx_figure_panel ltx_align_center"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2402.05290v2/model-free_comparisons.svg" id="S5.F5.sf2.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:318/139;" width="318" height="139"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">(b) </span>Learning curves compared to other baselines.</figcaption>
</figure></div></div>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 5: </span><span id="S5.F5.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Policy optimization with transformer AWMs gives better policies for long horizons.</span> (a) Final performance of BPO with different world models on Myriad (10 seeds <math id="S5.F5.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pm" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>±</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pm</annotation></semantics></math> 95% C.I.). (b) Learning curves of BPO through a transformer AWM, a SAC agent, and an Online-DT agent on 20 and 100 length horizons (10 seeds <math id="S5.F5.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pm" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>±</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pm</annotation></semantics></math> 95% C.I.).</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S5.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Figure <a href="#S5.F5.sf1" title="In Figure 5 ‣ 5.2 Benchmarking Credit Assignment with AWMs ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ Do Transformer World Models Give Better Policy Gradients?" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5a</span></a> shows the final performance of various world models used in BPO with increasing episode lengths. The transformer AWM is the only model to perform reliably well for increasingly long horizons, while other methods struggle when the horizon exceeds 100 steps. Indeed, when used as AWMs, transformer world models give better policy gradients than standard Markovian models and
RNN world models. However, when transformer world models are conditioned on states, their long-term policy gradients are no better than the gradients induced by Markovian models as measured by performance in Figure <a href="#S5.F5.sf1" title="In Figure 5 ‣ 5.2 Benchmarking Credit Assignment with AWMs ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ Do Transformer World Models Give Better Policy Gradients?" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5a</span></a>. These results corroborate our previous findings: transformer HWMs, RNN AWMs, and Markovian models all generate long policy gradient paths, which makes long-term credit assignment difficult.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS2.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">We also compare our method with other relevant baselines in Figure <a href="#S5.F5.sf2" title="In Figure 5 ‣ 5.2 Benchmarking Credit Assignment with AWMs ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ Do Transformer World Models Give Better Policy Gradients?" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5b</span></a>, namely model-free Soft Actor-Critic (SAC) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">Haarnoja et al. (2018)</a></cite> and the recently popularized Online Decision Transformer (Online-DT) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib57" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zheng et al. (2022)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib43" title="" class="ltx_ref">Schmidhuber (2019)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib48" title="" class="ltx_ref">Srivastava et al. (2019)</a></cite>. In addition to BPO with transformer AWMs scaling better with the problem horizon, BPO is also significantly more sample efficient than the two baselines.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S6" class="ltx_section">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">6 </span>Related Work</h3>

<div id="S6.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S6.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S6.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Backpropagation-based Policy Optimization</span>  
The concept of learning a policy by differentiating through the environment dynamics has been a foundational aspect of early RL methods <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib52" title="" class="ltx_ref">Werbos, 1974</a>; <a href="#bib.bib44" title="" class="ltx_ref">Schmidhuber, 1990</a>)</cite>. Estimators for such a policy gradient have been referred to with different names, including pathwise derivatives <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">Clavera et al., 2020</a>; <a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hafner et al., 2022</a>; <a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hafner et al., 2023</a>)</cite> and value gradients <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">Fairbank, 2014</a>; <a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">Heess et al., 2015</a>; <a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">Amos et al., 2021</a>)</cite>.
AWMs connect this literature to the one on sequence modeling with neural networks, with a focus on gradient propagation <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hochreiter, 1991</a>; <a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">Bengio et al., 1994</a>; <a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hochreiter, 1998</a>; <a href="#bib.bib38" title="" class="ltx_ref">Pascanu et al., 2013b</a>)</cite> and on architectures that allow for improved credit assignment <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hochreiter &amp; Schmidhuber, 1997</a>; <a href="#bib.bib50" title="" class="ltx_ref">Vaswani et al., 2017</a>; <a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kerg et al., 2020</a>)</cite>. Finally, our work can be seen as an instance of gradient-aware model-based RL <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">D’Oro et al., 2020</a>; <a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">D’Oro &amp; Jaskowski, 2020</a>; <a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Abachi et al., 2020</a>)</cite>, in which we modify the architecture of a model of the dynamics to obtain better policy gradients <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib31" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ma et al., 2021</a>)</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S6.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S6.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S6.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Multi-step state prediction with actions</span>  
Prior works used multi-step models related to AWMs, analyzing their role as partial models <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib41" title="" class="ltx_ref">Rezende et al., 2020</a>)</cite>, in the context of tree search <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib46" title="" class="ltx_ref">Schrittwieser et al., 2019</a>)</cite>, or training them with a multi-step latent prediction loss <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">Gregor et al., 2019</a>; <a href="#bib.bib47" title="" class="ltx_ref">Schwarzer et al., 2020</a>)</cite>, without however ever analyzing their gradient properties. Notably, models used in these prior works are rarely shown to work beyond a few dozen steps of unrolling or imagination, while AWMs demonstrably scale favorably for horizons well beyond established limitations.</p>
</div>
<div id="S6.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S6.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S6.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Sequence models in RL</span>  In partially observable MDPs, sequence models have been extensively used as history encoders to maximize returns with or without world models <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hausknecht &amp; Stone (2015)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib35" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ni et al. (2021)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hafner et al. (2023)</a></cite>. Other works have recently emerged treating MDPs as sequence modeling <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chen et al. (2021)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib57" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zheng et al. (2022)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">Janner et al. (2021)</a></cite>, in imitation learning or offline RL problem settings, based on return-conditioned models.
Sequence models have also been used to reshape rewards in sparse reward settings <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib24" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hung et al. (2019)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">Arjona-Medina et al. (2019)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib30" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liu et al. (2019)</a></cite>. In contrast to all of these, our framework uses an <span id="S6.p3.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">action-only</span> conditioned model to directly improve long-term policy gradients and naturally assigns credit by backpropagation as opposed to reward-shaping heuristics. Appendix <a href="#A7" title="Appendix G Extended Related Work on Sequence Models in RL ‣ Appendix ‣ Do Transformer World Models Give Better Policy Gradients?" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">G</span></a> contains a more detailed discussion of how all these methods differ from ours.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S7" class="ltx_section">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">7 </span>Conclusions and Limitations</h3>

<div id="S7.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S7.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We presented a model-based policy optimization framework based on
backpropagation through Actions World Models: models of the dynamics of the environment which only take an initial state and a sequence of actions as inputs.
We highlighted that, in contrast to the more common world models that compute the gradient by autoregressively unrolling their state predictions, AWMs do not suffer from the existence of circuitous gradient paths where the gradient can flow outside of the underlying network architecture.
We showed that their structure allows AWMs to fully exploit transformers’ favorable properties, taking advantage, both in theory and in practice, of their ability to perform long-term temporal credit assignment by leveraging short gradient paths.</p>
</div>
<div id="S7.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S7.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Theoretically, we demonstrated how transformer AWMs do not suffer from ill-behaved gradients coming from circuitous gradient paths which harm the quality of the gradients provided by more common Markovian models and HWMs.
Empirically, we showed that BPO using AWMs can be successful even when BPO using the underlying simulator fails, due to how AWMs leverage transformers’ inductive biases to obtain an easier-to-navigate policy optimization landscape.
We demonstrated that policies trained with transformer AWMs outperform existing model-based and model-free approaches, including recently proposed algorithms based on transformers, in realistic domains requiring long-term planning.</p>
</div>
<div id="S7.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S7.p3.1" class="ltx_p">While our theoretical analysis is developed within a deterministic setting, and our experiments are conducted in low-dimensional yet realistic domains, our framework establishes a new connection between gradient propagation techniques for sequence modeling and backpropagation-based policy gradients. Future work could focus on scaling our approach, making RL even more relevant to real-world applications where long-horizon capabilities are crucial.</p>
</div>

<p id="A1.p2.4" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.p2.4.1" class="ltx_text">In the recursive expansion of the previous line, notice the linear dependency w.r.t. <math id="A1.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="L_{a}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>L</mi><mi>a</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">L_{a}</annotation></semantics></math>, and exponential dependency w.r.t. <math id="A1.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="L_{s}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>L</mi><mi>s</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">L_{s}</annotation></semantics></math> due to the compounding products. Therefore, <math id="A1.p2.m7" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="\|\frac{dh(\hat{s}_{1:t},a_{1:t})}{da_{k}}\|=O(L_{a}+L_{s}^{t-k})\kern 5.0pt." display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo rspace="0.167em">∥</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>d</mi><mi>h</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>s</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><msub><mrow></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>a</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>k</mi></msub></mrow></mfrac><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0.0835em">∥</mo><mo lspace="0.0835em">=</mo><mi>O</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>L</mi><mi>a</mi></msub><mo>+</mo><msubsup><mi>L</mi><mi>s</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow></msubsup><mo rspace="0.222em" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\|\frac{dh(\hat{s}_{1:t},a_{1:t})}{da_{k}}\|=O(L_{a}+L_{s}^{t-k})\kern 5.0pt.</annotation></semantics></math>
We can then put everything together to derive the asymptotic behavior.</span></p>

<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_runin ltx_font_italic ltx_title_proof">Proof.</h6>
<div id="A1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.p4.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text">We begin by providing a formal definition of the recurrent network with its recurrent cell being the dynamics <math id="A1.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="f" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>f</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f</annotation></semantics></math> of the MDP as:</span></p>

<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="A1.Ex19.m2" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="\displaystyle:=f(s_{t-1},a_{t-1})=f(g_{f\text{-}\texttt{RNN}}(s_{1},a_{1:t-1}),a_{t})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo rspace="0em">:</mo><mo lspace="0em">=</mo><mi>f</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>f</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>g</mi><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mtext>-</mtext><mtext class="ltx_mathvariant_monospace">RNN</mtext></mrow></mrow></msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle:=f(s_{t-1},a_{t-1})=f(g_{f\text{-}\texttt{RNN}}(s_{1},a_{1:t-1}),a_{t})</annotation></semantics></math></td>

<p id="A1.p4.2" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.p4.2.1" class="ltx_text">Begin by developing the LHS of the equation.</span></p>

<p id="A1.p4.3" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.p4.3.1" class="ltx_text">where <math id="A1.p4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s_{t}=f(s_{t-1},a_{t-1})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s_{t}=f(s_{t-1},a_{t-1})</annotation></semantics></math> by construction (RNN assumption). Therefore, apply the chain rule <math id="A1.p4.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\frac{\partial s_{t}}{\partial a_{k}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mfrac><mrow><mo>∂</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow><mrow><mo>∂</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>k</mi></msub></mrow></mfrac><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{\partial s_{t}}{\partial a_{k}}</annotation></semantics></math>:</span></p>

<div id="A1.4" class="ltx_proof">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_runin ltx_font_italic ltx_title_proof">Proof.</h6>
<div id="A1.p6" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A1.p6.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.p6.1.1" class="ltx_text">With a slight abuse of notation, we use <math id="A1.p6.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="g_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>g</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">g_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> to replace <math id="A1.p6.m2" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="g(s_{1},a_{1:t-1})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>g</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">g(s_{1},a_{1:t-1})</annotation></semantics></math>.</span></p>
<table id="A1.Ex24" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A1.Ex24.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\nabla_{\bm{\theta}}J^{g}({\bm{\theta}};H)=\left\|\sum_{t=1}^{H}\frac{\partial r(\hat{s}_{t})}{\partial\hat{s}_{t}}\sum_{k=1}^{t-1}\frac{\partial g_{t}}{\partial a_{k}}\frac{\partial\pi(\hat{s}_{k})}{\partial{\bm{\theta}}}\right\|\leq L_{r}L_{\pi}\left\|\sum_{t=1}^{H}\sum_{k=1}^{t-1}\frac{\partial g_{t}}{\partial a_{k}}\right\|\leq L_{r}L_{\pi}\sum_{t=1}^{H}\sum_{k=1}^{t-1}\left\|\frac{\partial g_{t}}{\partial a_{k}}\right\|." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mrow><msub><mo>∇</mo><mi>𝜽</mi></msub><msup><mi>J</mi><mi>g</mi></msup></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝜽</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>H</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>‖</mo><mrow><munderover><mo lspace="0em" movablelimits="false">∑</mo><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>H</mi></munderover><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mo>∂</mo><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>s</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mrow><mo>∂</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>s</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow></mfrac><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><munderover><mo movablelimits="false">∑</mo><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></munderover><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mo>∂</mo><msub><mi>g</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow><mrow><mo>∂</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>k</mi></msub></mrow></mfrac><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mfrac><mrow><mo>∂</mo><mrow><mi>π</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>s</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>k</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mrow><mo>∂</mo><mi>𝜽</mi></mrow></mfrac></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>‖</mo></mrow><mo>≤</mo><mrow><msub><mi>L</mi><mi>r</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>L</mi><mi>π</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo>‖</mo><mrow><munderover><mo lspace="0em" movablelimits="false" rspace="0em">∑</mo><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>H</mi></munderover><mrow><munderover><mo movablelimits="false">∑</mo><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></munderover><mfrac><mrow><mo>∂</mo><msub><mi>g</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow><mrow><mo>∂</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>k</mi></msub></mrow></mfrac></mrow></mrow><mo>‖</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>≤</mo><mrow><msub><mi>L</mi><mi>r</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>L</mi><mi>π</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><munderover><mo movablelimits="false" rspace="0em">∑</mo><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>H</mi></munderover><mrow><munderover><mo movablelimits="false" rspace="0em">∑</mo><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></munderover><mrow><mo>‖</mo><mfrac><mrow><mo>∂</mo><msub><mi>g</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow><mrow><mo>∂</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>k</mi></msub></mrow></mfrac><mo>‖</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\nabla_{\bm{\theta}}J^{g}({\bm{\theta}};H)=\left\|\sum_{t=1}^{H}\frac{\partial r(\hat{s}_{t})}{\partial\hat{s}_{t}}\sum_{k=1}^{t-1}\frac{\partial g_{t}}{\partial a_{k}}\frac{\partial\pi(\hat{s}_{k})}{\partial{\bm{\theta}}}\right\|\leq L_{r}L_{\pi}\left\|\sum_{t=1}^{H}\sum_{k=1}^{t-1}\frac{\partial g_{t}}{\partial a_{k}}\right\|\leq L_{r}L_{\pi}\sum_{t=1}^{H}\sum_{k=1}^{t-1}\left\|\frac{\partial g_{t}}{\partial a_{k}}\right\|.</annotation></semantics></math></td>

<p id="A1.p6.2" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.p6.2.1" class="ltx_text">∎</span></p>

</div>
<div id="A1.p7" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.p7.1" class="ltx_p">See <a href="#Thmtheorem2.Thmcorollary1" title="Corollary 2.1. ‣ 4.2 Theoretical Properties of Actions World Models ‣ 4 Policy Gradient Computation with Actions World Models ‣ Do Transformer World Models Give Better Policy Gradients?" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2.1</span></a></p>
</div>
<div id="A1.5" class="ltx_proof">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_runin ltx_font_italic ltx_title_proof">Proof.</h6>
<div id="A1.p8" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A1.p8.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.p8.1.1" class="ltx_text">We begin by defining the transition function of the recurrent network as <math id="A1.p8.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x_{t}=\sigma(W_{x}x_{t-1})+W_{a}a_{t}+b" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>σ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>W</mi><mi>x</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><msub><mi>W</mi><mi>a</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x_{t}=\sigma(W_{x}x_{t-1})+W_{a}a_{t}+b</annotation></semantics></math>, where <math id="A1.p8.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sigma" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>σ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sigma</annotation></semantics></math> is some activation function with gradient norm bounded by <math id="A1.p8.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\left\|diag(\sigma^{\prime}(x))\right\|\leq\frac{1}{\beta}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mo>‖</mo><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>a</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>g</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msup><mi>σ</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>‖</mo></mrow><mo>≤</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mi>β</mi></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\left\|diag(\sigma^{\prime}(x))\right\|\leq\frac{1}{\beta}</annotation></semantics></math>. Further, consider a linear output cell <math id="A1.p8.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s_{t+1}=W_{o}x_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>s</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>W</mi><mi>o</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s_{t+1}=W_{o}x_{t}</annotation></semantics></math>. Now we begin by showing that <math id="A1.p8.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\left\|\frac{\partial x_{t}}{\partial a_{k}}\right\|\leq||W_{a}^{T}||(||W_{x}^{T}||\frac{1}{\beta})^{t-k}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mo>‖</mo><mfrac><mrow><mo>∂</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow><mrow><mo>∂</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>k</mi></msub></mrow></mfrac><mo>‖</mo></mrow><mo>≤</mo><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><msubsup><mi>W</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>T</mi></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><msubsup><mi>W</mi><mi>x</mi><mi>T</mi></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mi>β</mi></mfrac></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow></msup></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\left\|\frac{\partial x_{t}}{\partial a_{k}}\right\|\leq||W_{a}^{T}||(||W_{x}^{T}||\frac{1}{\beta})^{t-k}</annotation></semantics></math>:</span></p>
</div>

<div id="A1.p10" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.p10.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.p10.1.1" class="ltx_text">We develop the expression <math id="A1.p10.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\frac{\partial\hat{s}_{t}}{\partial a_{k}}=\frac{\partial\hat{s}_{t}}{\partial x_{t-1}}\frac{\partial x_{t-1}}{\partial a_{k}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mo>∂</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>s</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow><mrow><mo>∂</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>k</mi></msub></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mo>∂</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>s</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow><mrow><mo>∂</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></mfrac><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mfrac><mrow><mo>∂</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow><mrow><mo>∂</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>k</mi></msub></mrow></mfrac></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{\partial\hat{s}_{t}}{\partial a_{k}}=\frac{\partial\hat{s}_{t}}{\partial x_{t-1}}\frac{\partial x_{t-1}}{\partial a_{k}}</annotation></semantics></math>, applying the norm and plugging in the above result we obtain:</span></p>
