<p id="A1.p10.2" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.p10.2.1" class="ltx_text">We then use the bound found in Theorem 1:</span></p>
<table id="A1.EGx18" class="ltx_equationgroup ltx_eqn_align ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody id="A1.Ex31"><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="A1.Ex31.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle\left\|\nabla_{\bm{\theta}}J^{g}({\bm{\theta}};H)\right\|" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>‖</mo><mrow><mrow><msub><mo rspace="0.167em">∇</mo><mi>𝜽</mi></msub><msup><mi>J</mi><mi>g</mi></msup></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝜽</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>H</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>‖</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle\left\|\nabla_{\bm{\theta}}J^{g}({\bm{\theta}};H)\right\|</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="A1.Ex31.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle\leq L_{r}L_{\pi}\sum_{t=1}^{H}\sum_{k=1}^{t-1}\left\|\frac{\partial g_{t}}{\partial a_{k}}\right\|=L_{r}L_{\pi}\sum_{t=1}^{H}\sum_{k=1}^{t-1}\left\|\frac{\partial\hat{s}_{t}}{\partial a_{k}}\right\|" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>≤</mo><mrow><msub><mi>L</mi><mi>r</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>L</mi><mi>π</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mstyle displaystyle="true"><munderover><mo movablelimits="false">∑</mo><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>H</mi></munderover></mstyle><mrow><mstyle <div id="A1.6" class="ltx_proof">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_runin ltx_font_italic ltx_title_proof">Proof.</h6>
<div id="A1.p12" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A1.p12.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.p12.1.1" class="ltx_text">We begin with the definition of the self-attention Actions World Model. Let <math id="A1.p12.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="Q\in\mathbb{R}^{1\times d_{z}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>Q</mi><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>z</mi></msub></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">Q\in\mathbb{R}^{1\times d_{z}}</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="A1.p12.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d_{z}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>z</mi></msub></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d_{z}}</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="A1.p12.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="V\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d_{o}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>V</mi><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>o</mi></msub></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">V\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d_{o}}</annotation></semantics></math>, attention can be defined as :</span></p>
<table id="A1.Ex36" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A1.Ex36.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\text{Attention}(Q,K,V):=\text{softmax}(QK^{T})V" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mtext>Attention</mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>Q</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>K</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>V</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>:=</mo><mrow><mtext>softmax</mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>Q</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>K</mi><mi>T</mi></msup></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>V</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\text{Attention}(Q,K,V):=\text{softmax}(QK^{T})V</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div>
<div id="A1.p13" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A1.p13.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.p13.1.1" class="ltx_text">A self-attention AWM can then be defined in the following way with weight matrices <math id="A1.p13.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W_{q}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{z}\times d_{a}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>W</mi><mi>q</mi></msub><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mrow><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>z</mi></msub><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>a</mi></msub></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W_{q}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{z}\times d_{a}}</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="A1.p13.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W_{k}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{z}\times d_{a}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>W</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mrow><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>z</mi></msub><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>a</mi></msub></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W_{k}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{z}\times d_{a}}</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="A1.p13.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W_{v}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{s}\times d_{a}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>W</mi><mi>v</mi></msub><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mrow><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>s</mi></msub><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>a</mi></msub></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W_{v}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{s}\times d_{a}}</annotation></semantics></math>.</span></p>
</div>
<div id="A1.p14" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<table id="A1.Ex37" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A1.Ex37.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="\texttt{ATT}_{t}(a_{1},...a_{t-1}):=\text{Attention}(a_{t-1}W_{q}^{T},a_{1:t-1}W_{k}^{T},a_{1:t-1}W_{v}^{T})=\sum_{i=1}^{t-1}c_{i}(a_{i}W_{v}^{T})\kern 5.0pt=\hat{s}_{t}," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mtext class="ltx_mathvariant_monospace">ATT</mtext><mi>t</mi></msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>:=</mo><mtext>Attention</mtext><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><msubsup><mi>W</mi><mi>q</mi><mi>T</mi></msubsup><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mrow></msub><msubsup><mi>W</mi><mi>k</mi><mi>T</mi></msubsup><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mrow></msub><msubsup><mi>W</mi><mi>v</mi><mi>T</mi></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo rspace="0.111em">=</mo><munderover><mo movablelimits="false">∑</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></munderover><msub><mi>c</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><msubsup><mi>W</mi><mi>v</mi><mi>T</mi></msubsup><mo rspace="0.500em" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>s</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\texttt{ATT}_{t}(a_{1},...a_{t-1}):=\text{Attention}(a_{t-1}W_{q}^{T},a_{1:t-1}W_{k}^{T},a_{1:t-1}W_{v}^{T})=\sum_{i=1}^{t-1}c_{i}(a_{i}W_{v}^{T})\kern 5.0pt=\hat{s}_{t},</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div>
<div id="A1.p15" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A1.p15.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.p15.1.1" class="ltx_text">where <math id="A1.p15.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="c_{i}=\text{softmax}_{i}(a_{t-1}W_{q}^{T}W_{k}a_{1:t-1}^{T})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>c</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mtext>softmax</mtext><mi>i</mi></msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><msubsup><mi>W</mi><mi>q</mi><mi>T</mi></msubsup><msub><mi>W</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><msubsup><mi>a</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mrow><mi>T</mi></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">c_{i}=\text{softmax}_{i}(a_{t-1}W_{q}^{T}W_{k}a_{1:t-1}^{T})</annotation></semantics></math>. The subscript on the softmax operator indicates the <math id="A1.p15.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="i" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>i</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">i</annotation></semantics></math>th index. Now, we begin by showing the expression for <math id="A1.p15.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\frac{\partial g_{t}}{\partial a_{k}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mfrac><mrow><mo>∂</mo><msub><mi>g</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow><mrow><mo>∂</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>k</mi></msub></mrow></mfrac><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{\partial g_{t}}{\partial a_{k}}</annotation></semantics></math>:</span></p>
<table id="A1.EGx20" class="ltx_equationgroup ltx_eqn_align ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody id="A1.Ex38"><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">

<section id="A1.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">A.1 </span>Tightness of Theorem <a href="#Thmtheorem1" title="Theorem 1. ‣ 3 Policy Gradient Computation with History World Models ‣ Do Transformer World Models Give Better Policy Gradients?" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a></h4>

<div id="A1.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The result of Theorem <a href="#Thmtheorem1" title="Theorem 1. ‣ 3 Policy Gradient Computation with History World Models ‣ Do Transformer World Models Give Better Policy Gradients?" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a> argues that policy gradients computed through equation <a href="#S3.E2" title="In 3 Policy Gradient Computation with History World Models ‣ Do Transformer World Models Give Better Policy Gradients?" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a> may explode as the horizon grows. To make this claim, we comment on the tightness of the upper bound provided in Theorem <a href="#Thmtheorem1" title="Theorem 1. ‣ 3 Policy Gradient Computation with History World Models ‣ Do Transformer World Models Give Better Policy Gradients?" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>. Consider the one-dimensional case, where all the gradients are positive scalars, and <math id="A1.SS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="\|\frac{\partial h(\hat{s}_{1:t},a_{1:t})}{\partial a_{k}}\|=L_{a}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo rspace="0.167em">∥</mo><mfrac><mrow><mo>∂</mo><mi>h</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>s</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><msub><mrow></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>a</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mo>∂</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>k</mi></msub></mrow></mfrac><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0.0835em">∥</mo><mo lspace="0.0835em">=</mo><mi>L</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mi>a</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\|\frac{\partial h(\hat{s}_{1:t},a_{1:t})}{\partial a_{k}}\|=L_{a}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="A1.SS1.p1.m2" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="\|\frac{\partial h(\hat{s}_{1:t},a_{1:t})}{\partial\hat{s}_{i}}\|=L_{s}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo rspace="0.167em">∥</mo><mfrac><mrow><mo>∂</mo><mi>h</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>s</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><msub><mrow></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>a</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mo>∂</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>s</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></mfrac><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0.0835em">∥</mo><mo lspace="0.0835em">=</mo><mi>L</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mi>s</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\|\frac{\partial h(\hat{s}_{1:t},a_{1:t})}{\partial\hat{s}_{i}}\|=L_{s}</annotation></semantics></math> for all <math id="A1.SS1.p1.m3" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="\hat{s}_{1:t},a_{1:t},k,i" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>s</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><msub><mrow></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>a</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>k</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{s}_{1:t},a_{1:t},k,i</annotation></semantics></math>. Then, we show that</p>

<div id="A1.SS1.2" class="ltx_proof">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_runin ltx_font_italic ltx_title_proof">Proof.</h6>
<div id="A1.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.SS1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text">We begin the proof of this lower bound in a similar way, by considering only one of the terms of the summation. For clarity, Let <math id="A1.SS1.p2.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="h_{i}=h(\hat{s}_{1:i-1},a_{1:i-1})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>h</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>h</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>s</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">h_{i}=h(\hat{s}_{1:i-1},a_{1:i-1})</annotation></semantics></math>.</span></p>

<p id="A1.SS1.p2.3" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.SS1.p2.3.1" class="ltx_text">∎</span></p>
</div>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A1.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">A.2 </span>Tightness of Corollary <a href="#S4.EGx5" title="Corollary 2.1. ‣ 4.2 Theoretical Properties of Actions World Models ‣ 4 Policy Gradient Computation with Actions World Models ‣ Do Transformer World Models Give Better Policy Gradients?" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2.1</span></a></h4>

<div id="A1.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The result of Corollary <a href="#S4.EGx5" title="Corollary 2.1. ‣ 4.2 Theoretical Properties of Actions World Models ‣ 4 Policy Gradient Computation with Actions World Models ‣ Do Transformer World Models Give Better Policy Gradients?" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2.1</span></a> argues that policy gradients through Markovian models may explode as the horizon grows. In order to make this claim, we comment on the tightness of the bound. Just like for Theorem <a href="#Thmtheorem1" title="Theorem 1. ‣ 3 Policy Gradient Computation with History World Models ‣ Do Transformer World Models Give Better Policy Gradients?" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>, consider the one-dimensional case, where all the gradients are positive scalars and assume further the gradient norm of the activation function <math id="A1.SS2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sigma" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>σ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sigma</annotation></semantics></math> is lower bounded by <math id="A1.SS2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\gamma&gt;0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>γ</mi><mo>&gt;</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\gamma&gt;0</annotation></semantics></math> (which is the case for popular activation functions such as sigmoid). We will show that, given these conditions, the bound can be written as a lower bound:</p>
<table id="A1.EGx26" class="ltx_equationgroup ltx_eqn_align ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody id="A1.Ex56"><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="A1.Ex56.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle\|\nabla_{\bm{\theta}}J^{g_{\texttt{RNN}}}({\bm{\theta}};H)\|=\Omega(\eta^{H})\kern 5.0pt." display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><mrow><mrow><msub><mo rspace="0.167em">∇</mo><mi>𝜽</mi></msub><msup><mi>J</mi><msub><mi>g</mi><mtext class="ltx_mathvariant_monospace">RNN</mtext></msub></msup></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝜽</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>H</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Ω</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>η</mi><mi>H</mi></msup><mo rspace="0.222em" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle\|\nabla_{\bm{\theta}}J^{g_{\texttt{RNN}}}({\bm{\theta}};H)\|=\Omega(\eta^{H})\kern 5.0pt.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div>
<div id="A1.SS2.2" class="ltx_proof">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_runin ltx_font_italic ltx_title_proof">Proof.</h6>
<div id="A1.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.SS2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text">We begin the proof by lower bounding the expression for the recurrent cell <math id="A1.SS2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\frac{\partial x_{t}}{\partial a_{k}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mfrac><mrow><mo>∂</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow><mrow><mo>∂</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>k</mi></msub></mrow></mfrac><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{\partial x_{t}}{\partial a_{k}}</annotation></semantics></math>:</span></p>
<table id="A1.EGx27" class="ltx_equationgroup ltx_eqn_align ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody id="A1.Ex57"><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="A1.Ex57.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle\frac{\partial x_{t}}{\partial a_{k}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mstyle displaystyle="true"><mfrac><mrow><mo>∂</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow><mrow><mo>∂</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>k</mi></msub></mrow></mfrac></mstyle><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle\frac{\partial x_{t}}{\partial a_{k}}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="A1.Ex57.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle\geq||W_{a}^{T}||(||W_{x}^{T}||\gamma)^{t-k}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>≥</mo><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><msubsup><mi>W</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>T</mi></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><msubsup><mi>W</mi><mi>x</mi><mi>T</mi></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>γ</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow></msup></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle\geq||W_{a}^{T}||(||W_{x}^{T}||\gamma)^{t-k}</annotation></semantics></math></td>

<p id="A1.SS2.p2.2" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.SS2.p2.2.1" class="ltx_text">The bound found in Theorem <a href="#Thmtheorem2" title="Theorem 2. ‣ 4.2 Theoretical Properties of Actions World Models ‣ 4 Policy Gradient Computation with Actions World Models ‣ Do Transformer World Models Give Better Policy Gradients?" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a> can also be rewritten as an equality given these additional assumptions, since the Cauchy-Schwarz and triangle inequalities become equalities in the one-dimensional positive case: <math id="A1.SS2.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\|\nabla_{\bm{\theta}}J^{g}({\bm{\theta}};H)\|=L_{r}L_{\pi}\sum_{t=1}^{H}\sum_{k=1}^{t-1}\left\|\frac{\partial g_{t}}{\partial a_{k}}\right\|" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><mrow><mrow><msub><mo rspace="0.167em">∇</mo><mi>𝜽</mi></msub><msup><mi>J</mi><mi>g</mi></msup></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝜽</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>H</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>L</mi><mi>r</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>L</mi><mi>π</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><msubsup><mo rspace="0em">∑</mo><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>H</mi></msubsup><mrow><msubsup><mo rspace="0em">∑</mo><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msubsup><mrow><mo>‖</mo><mfrac><mrow><mo>∂</mo><msub><mi>g</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow><mrow><mo>∂</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>k</mi></msub></mrow></mfrac><mo>‖</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\|\nabla_{\bm{\theta}}J^{g}({\bm{\theta}};H)\|=L_{r}L_{\pi}\sum_{t=1}^{H}\sum_{k=1}^{t-1}\left\|\frac{\partial g_{t}}{\partial a_{k}}\right\|</annotation></semantics></math>. Finally, putting these new results together, we find that</span></p>

<section id="A2" class="ltx_appendix">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix B </span>Training an AWM with Teacher Forcing</h3>

<div id="A2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The policy gradient framework provided by Actions World Models can also be used to interpret training design choices used in RL through the lens of sequence modeling.
As a concrete example, recall that the transition function of a Markovian model can be trained with the following loss:</p>
<table id="A2.EGx29" class="ltx_equationgroup ltx_eqn_align ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody id="A2.E6"><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="A2.E6.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle\ell^{\hat{f}}(\tau;{\bm{\psi}})=\sum_{t=1}^{H-1}\|s_{t+1}^{\tau}-\hat{f}_{\bm{\psi}}(s_{t}^{\tau},a_{t}^{\tau})\|^{2}\kern 5.0pt." display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><msup><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>^</mo></mover></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>τ</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>𝝍</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mstyle displaystyle="true"><munderover><mo movablelimits="false">∑</mo><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>H</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></munderover></mstyle><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><mrow><msubsup><mi>s</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>τ</mi></msubsup><mo>−</mo><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>𝝍</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mi>s</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>τ</mi></msubsup><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mi>a</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>τ</mi></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle\ell^{\hat{f}}(\tau;{\bm{\psi}})=\sum_{t=1}^{H-1}\|s_{t+1}^{\tau}-\hat{f}_{\bm{\psi}}(s_{t}^{\tau},a_{t}^{\tau})\|^{2}\kern 5.0pt.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(6)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="A2.p1.2" class="ltx_p">We present the following remark.</p>
</div>
<div id="Thmremark1" class="ltx_theorem ltx_theorem_remark">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_runin ltx_title_theorem"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_theorem"><span id="Thmremark1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Remark 1</span></span><span id="Thmremark1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">.</span></h6>
<div id="Thmremark1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Thmremark1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="Thmremark1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Training an AWM instantiated with an RNN to predict states using teacher forcing is equivalent to training its recurrent cell with the loss function from Equation <a href="#A2.E6" title="In Appendix B Training an AWM with Teacher Forcing ‣ Appendix ‣ Do Transformer World Models Give Better Policy Gradients?" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a>.</span></p>
</div>
</div>
<div id="A2.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Teacher forcing <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib53" title="" class="ltx_ref">Williams &amp; Zipser, 1989</a>)</cite> is an algorithm used to train recurrent neural networks. Instead of autoregressively unrolling them during training, it enforces the outputs (i.e., in this case, the environment/RNN states) to be the ones coming from a ground-truth sequence.
In other words, when training an AWM as an RNN with teacher forcing, we are essentially training its recurrent cell as a one-step model, as traditionally done in model-based RL applied to a Markovian setting.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A3" class="ltx_appendix">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix C </span>Reinforcement Learning Hyperparameters</h3>

<section id="A3.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">C.1 </span>Model-based Hyperparameters</h4>

<div id="A3.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A3.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">All model-based backpropagation-based policy optimization methods, including the Markovian agent, AWMs and HWMs were sweeped on three entropy constants for exploration: <math id="A3.SS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="[0.1,0.01,0.001]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mn>0.1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>0.01</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>0.001</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">[0.1,0.01,0.001]</annotation></semantics></math>, and the best performing results are reported. Indeed, in addition to the objective function <math id="A3.SS1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="J" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>J</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">J</annotation></semantics></math>, the policies are optimized with an additional entropy maximization factor as done in <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">Amos et al. (2021)</a></cite> for exploration. All actions, and states (for History World Models) are embedded with a linear layer with an output size of 72. The RNN is initialized with two hidden layers, with a hidden layer size of (64, 64). The self-attention transformers use a similar architecture to the GPT-2 model <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib39" title="" class="ltx_ref">Radford et al., 2019</a>)</cite> implemented by the Hugging Face Transformer library <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib54" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wolf et al., 2019</a>)</cite>. Our transformers stack 2 layers and 3 heads of self-attention modules, with hidden layers of size 64. Timesteps are added as an input to every input of all world models, since we are in a finite-horizon setting. The Markovian world models predicts transitions as a difference function: <math id="A3.SS1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{s}_{t}=\hat{f}(s_{t-1},a_{t-1})+s_{t-1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>s</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{s}_{t}=\hat{f}(s_{t-1},a_{t-1})+s_{t-1}</annotation></semantics></math>, using two hidden layers of size (64, 64), and ReLU activation functions. Gradient norms are clipped at a value of 100 for all policy gradients. All other hyper-parameters relating to the policy learning algorithm are shown in Table <a href="#A3.T1" title="Table 1 ‣ C.1 Model-based Hyperparameters ‣ Appendix C Reinforcement Learning Hyperparameters ‣ Appendix ‣ Do Transformer World Models Give Better Policy Gradients?" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>.</p>
</div>

<section id="A3.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">C.2 </span>Model-free Hyperparameters</h4>

<div id="A3.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A3.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We use a model-free soft-actor critic <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">Haarnoja et al. (2018)</a></cite> as a benchmark for the myriad experiments. The critic of this agent is modeled as a 2-layer MLP with 256 hidden units each. Entropy regularization is done using a constant entropy constant. Results in Figure <a href="#S5.F5.sf2" title="In Figure 5 ‣ 5.2 Benchmarking Credit Assignment with AWMs ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ Do Transformer World Models Give Better Policy Gradients?" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5b</span></a> show the best performing results after doing a grid search over the following hyper-parameters: learning rate <math id="A3.SS2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="=[0.001,0.0001,0.00001]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mn>0.001</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>0.0001</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>0.00001</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">=[0.001,0.0001,0.00001]</annotation></semantics></math> and entropy constant <math id="A3.SS2.p1.m2" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="=[1.,0.01,0.001]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mn>1</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0.167em">.</mo><mo>,</mo><mn>0.01</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>0.001</mn><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">=[1.,0.01,0.001]</annotation></semantics></math>. The remaining hyperparameters are shown in Table <a href="#A3.T2" title="Table 2 ‣ C.2 Model-free Hyperparameters ‣ Appendix C Reinforcement Learning Hyperparameters ‣ Appendix ‣ Do Transformer World Models Give Better Policy Gradients?" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>.</p>
</div>

<section id="A4" class="ltx_appendix">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix D </span>Offline Experiments</h3>

<div id="A4.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The experiments showed in Figure <a href="#S4.F3" title="Figure 3 ‣ 4.2 Theoretical Properties of Actions World Models ‣ 4 Policy Gradient Computation with Actions World Models ‣ Do Transformer World Models Give Better Policy Gradients?" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a> and Figure <a href="#S5.F4" title="Figure 4 ‣ 5.1 Empirical Properties of Action World Models ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ Do Transformer World Models Give Better Policy Gradients?" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a> are in the offline setting. In both settings, 100000 transitions are collected for all experiments using a uniform random policy. The world models are then trained on data sampled from these transitions for 1000 steps. The batch size and learning rate are set to the same values as shown in Table <a href="#A3.T1" title="Table 1 ‣ C.1 Model-based Hyperparameters ‣ Appendix C Reinforcement Learning Hyperparameters ‣ Appendix ‣ Do Transformer World Models Give Better Policy Gradients?" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A5" class="ltx_appendix">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix E </span>Online Double-pendulum Experiments</h3>

<div id="A5.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The goal position of the environment is calculated using some fixed initial angular position (initial action) for all episode lengths. In our experiments, the optimal action is -0.4, which corresponds to an initial angle of <math id="A5.p1.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="-0.4\times 180^{\circ}." display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>0.4</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mn>180</mn><msup><mrow></mrow><mo>∘</mo></msup><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">-0.4\times 180^{\circ}.</annotation></semantics></math> The results in the double-pendulum experiments use the same hype-parameters as the Myriad experiments, with two exceptions: the number of environment steps used for optimization is 100000 instead of 200000, and the leaerning rate is sweeped for values in [0.01, 0.001, 0.0001, 0.00001, 0.000001] due to the unstable gradients. The complete learning curves are shown in Figure <a href="#A5.F6" title="Figure 6 ‣ Appendix E Online Double-pendulum Experiments ‣ Appendix ‣ Do Transformer World Models Give Better Policy Gradients?" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<figure id="A5.F6" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2402.05290v2/double-pend-rl-curves.svg" id="A5.F6.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:494/103;" width="494" height="103"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 6: </span>Learning curves of different world models used for BPO on the double-pendulum environment for different horizons. The horizons presented are <math id="A5.F6.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="H=[5,10,20,50,100]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>H</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mn>5</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>10</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>20</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>50</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>100</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">H=[5,10,20,50,100]</annotation></semantics></math> in order (10 seeds <math id="A5.F6.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pm" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>±</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pm</annotation></semantics></math> std).</figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="A6" class="ltx_appendix">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix F </span>Myriad Environments</h3>

<div id="A6.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A6.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We give a short overview of each of the Myriad environments used in this work. For more details, refer to <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">Howe et al. (2022)</a></cite> and <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib29" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lenhart &amp; Workman (2007)</a></cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="A6.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A6.p2.1" class="ltx_p">The underlying dynamics of each of these environments are described by a set of ordinary differential equations, which are then discretized using Euler’s method for discrete-time optimal control. In practice, to change a problem’s horizon, we fix the duration of the experiment to ensure it is still interesting and simply discretize using a smaller or larger step size.
We normalize the returns, where <math id="A6.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0</annotation></semantics></math> is the expected performance of a random policy and <math id="A6.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>1</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1</annotation></semantics></math> is the performance of an optimal policy provided by <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">Howe et al. (2022)</a></cite><span id="footnote5" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">5</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">5</sup>
              <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">5</span>



            Optimal policies are computed using trajectory optimization on the underlying differential equations.</span></span></span>. Our experiments are conducted on eight environments: <span id="A6.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">cancer treatment, bioreactor, mould fungicide, bacteria, harvest, invasive plant, HIV treatment,</span> and <span id="A6.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">timber harvest</span>. Each environment’s state and action space varies between one and five dimensions.</p>
</div>
<div id="A6.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A6.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A6.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Cancer treatment</span> follows the normalized density of a cancerous tumour undergoing chemotherapy. The actions at every time step correspond to the strength of the chemotherapy drug at a given time. The goal is to minimize the size of the tumour over a set fixed duration while also minimizing the amount of drugs administered to the patient.</p>
</div>
<div id="A6.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A6.p4.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A6.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Bioreactor</span> seeks to minimize the total amount of a chemical contaminant that naturally degrades in the presence of bacteria. The actions here allow the agent to feed the bacteria, increasing its population and increasing the rate of the contaminants’ degradation. However, a cost is associated with feeding the bacteria.</p>
</div>
<div id="A6.p5" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A6.p5.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A6.p5.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Mould fungicide</span> models the concentration of a mould population. The goal is to minimize its population by applying a fungicide, which has an associated cost to apply.</p>
</div>
<div id="A6.p6" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A6.p6.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A6.p6.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Bacteria</span> looks to maximize a bacteria population through the application of a chemical nutrient that stimulates growth. On top of the associated cost of applying the chemical nutrient, the chemical also produces a byproduct that might, in turn, hinder bacterial growth.</p>
</div>
<div id="A6.p7" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A6.p7.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A6.p7.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Harvest</span> models the growing population of some vegetables, and the goal is to maximize the harvested yield of this population. While harvesting directly contributes to the reward, it consequently slows down the population’s exponential growth.</p>
</div>
<div id="A6.p8" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A6.p8.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A6.p8.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Invasive plant</span> seeks to minimize the presence of an invasive plant species through interventions that remove a proportion of the invasive population. These actions have an associated cost.</p>
</div>
<div id="A6.p9" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A6.p9.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A6.p9.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">HIV treatment</span> follows the evolution of uninfected and infected cells in the presence of a virus. The actions correspond to a drug administered that affects the virus’ rate of infection. The use of the drug must also be minimized.</p>
</div>
<div id="A6.p10" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A6.p10.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A6.p10.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Timber harvest</span> is similar to the harvest environment, except the harvested population is infinite. Instead, harvested timber can be converted into capital, which can then be re-invested in the harvesting operation, stimulating company growth. The goal is to maximize revenue.</p>
</div>
<div id="A6.p11" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A6.p11.1" class="ltx_p">To the best of our knowledge, this paper presents the first results using reinforcement learning for the environments in Myriad. The final performances of all BPO methods and the SAC agent for each of the eight environments are shown in Figures <a href="#A6.F7" title="Figure 7 ‣ Appendix F Myriad Environments ‣ Appendix ‣ Do Transformer World Models Give Better Policy Gradients?" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">7</span></a>. Note that not only does our method (BPO with transformer AWM) have the best aggregate scores for long horizons, but it also achieves the best performance for the longest horizon of 500 steps for each environment.</p>
</div>
<figure id="A6.F7" class="ltx_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_1"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2402.05290v2/individual_aggregate_myriad.svg" id="A6.F7.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_figure_panel ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:521/202;" width="521" height="202"></object></div></div>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 7: </span><span id="A6.F7.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Policy gradients through transformer AWMs give better policies for long horizons for every environment. </span> Learning curves of BPO with different world models on eight of the Myriad environments (10 seeds <math id="A6.F7.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pm" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>±</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pm</annotation></semantics></math> min/max)</figcaption><div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_1">
<p id="A6.F7.4" class="ltx_p ltx_figure_panel ltx_align_center">.</p></div></div>
</figure>
<section id="A6.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">F.1 </span>Ablation on Stop Gradient</h4>

<div id="A6.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A6.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Most of the analysis in this work relies on the assumption that the gradient is stopped through the policy input, as seen in equation <a href="#S2.E1" title="In 2 Background ‣ Do Transformer World Models Give Better Policy Gradients?" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>, equation <a href="#S3.E2" title="In 3 Policy Gradient Computation with History World Models ‣ Do Transformer World Models Give Better Policy Gradients?" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a> and equation <a href="#S4.E4" title="In 4.2 Theoretical Properties of Actions World Models ‣ 4 Policy Gradient Computation with Actions World Models ‣ Do Transformer World Models Give Better Policy Gradients?" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>. Just like it was noted in prior work <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hafner et al. (2022)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hafner et al. (2023)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ghugare et al. (2023)</a></cite>, we also perform an ablation on whether the stop-gradient operator on the policy input has any major impact on the final performance on the Myriad benchmark. The results in Figure <a href="#A6.F8" title="Figure 8 ‣ F.1 Ablation on Stop Gradient ‣ Appendix F Myriad Environments ‣ Appendix ‣ Do Transformer World Models Give Better Policy Gradients?" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">8</span></a> confirm previous remarks that detaching the policy input from the policy gradient has little to no effect on final performance.</p>
</div>
<figure id="A6.F8" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2402.05290v2/aggregate_iqm_fullgrad.svg" id="A6.F8.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:274/196;" width="274" height="196"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 8: </span><span id="A6.F8.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Stop gradients on the policy input do not affect final performances on the Myriad benchmark.</span> Final performances of BPO with a transformer AWM and a transformer HWM, with and without the full policy gradient (10 seeds <math id="A6.F8.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pm" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>±</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pm</annotation></semantics></math> 95% C.I.). <em id="A6.F8.6" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">Stop Grad</em> denotes the policy gradient used throughout the main text of this paper, while <em id="A6.F8.7" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">Full Grad</em> denotes the full unbiased policy gradient without any stop gradient operators.</figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="A6.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">F.2 </span>Ablation on LSTMs</h4>

<div id="A6.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A6.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Our analysis suggests that policy gradients through an AWM inherit certain gradient properties of the underlying world model architecture. Long-short-term memory networks (LSTMs) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hochreiter (1998)</a></cite> were also suggested as an alternative to vanilla RNNs due to their favorable long-term gradients. Indeed, we show in an ablation study that LSTM AWMs also perform quite well on the Myriad benchmark in Figure <a href="#A6.F9" title="Figure 9 ‣ F.2 Ablation on LSTMs ‣ Appendix F Myriad Environments ‣ Appendix ‣ Do Transformer World Models Give Better Policy Gradients?" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">9</span></a>. Thus, the Actions World Model is agnostic to the specific neural network architecture, allowing any modern sequence models to produce favorable policy gradients, which could be an interesting direction to explore other more advanced sequence models such as state space models <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">Gu et al. (2022)</a></cite>. We hypothesize that LSTMs are quite effective on environments from Myriad due to the recurrent inductive bias that is compatible with all MDPs. We suspect transformer AWMs show greater promise for large-scale experiments, especially in POMDPs.</p>
</div>
<figure id="A6.F9" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2402.05290v2/individual_hist_lstm.svg" id="A6.F9.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:494/228;" width="494" height="228"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 9: </span><span id="A6.F9.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Ablation with LSTM Actions World Models on Myriad</span>. Learning curves of BPO with a transformer AWM, LSTM AWM, and a Markovian world model on eight of the Myriad environments (10 seeds <math id="A6.F9.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pm" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>±</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pm</annotation></semantics></math> min/max).</figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="A6.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">F.3 </span>Additional Details on Online Decision Transformer</h4>

<div id="A6.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A6.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Recently, a sequence modeling perspective of reinforcement learning has shown promising results on various continuous control tasks in an offline RL setting <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chen et al., 2021</a>; <a href="#bib.bib57" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zheng et al., 2022</a>; <a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">Janner et al., 2021</a>)</cite>. Although our method differs significantly both conceptually and in the problems they solve (see Appendix <a href="#A7" title="Appendix G Extended Related Work on Sequence Models in RL ‣ Appendix ‣ Do Transformer World Models Give Better Policy Gradients?" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">G</span></a>), we show experimentally, for completeness, that the online decision transformer <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib57" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zheng et al., 2022</a>)</cite> performs poorly on the low dimensional Myriad suite. We use the code and hyperparameters provided by <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib57" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zheng et al. (2022)</a></cite> in a purely online setup, with a sweep on the number of trajectories gathered per iteration due to the online nature of our problem setup. Importantly, decision transformers (DT) must be conditioned on the <span id="A6.SS3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">return-to-go</span> (RTG) to derive desired policies. Prior works <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chen et al., 2021</a>; <a href="#bib.bib57" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zheng et al., 2022</a>; <a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">Janner et al., 2021</a>)</cite> have shown that DTs are robust to these hyperparameters and can achieve good and sometimes better performance even when the RTG is set to an out-of-distribution return that is impossible to attain.</p>
</div>
<div id="A6.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A6.SS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">We show in Figure <a href="#A6.F10" title="Figure 10 ‣ F.3 Additional Details on Online Decision Transformer ‣ Appendix F Myriad Environments ‣ Appendix ‣ Do Transformer World Models Give Better Policy Gradients?" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">10</span></a> that DT performs poorly on the Myriad tasks in an online setting. We summarize some of the takeaways from these experiments:</p>
<ul id="A6.I1" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="A6.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span>
<div id="A6.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A6.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Decision transformers are still not well suited for a purely online training regime, exhibiting worse performance than simple one-step model-based methods. Moreover, the action-sequence model outperforms the decision transformer in every single environment.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="A6.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span>
<div id="A6.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A6.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Decision transformers require some expert knowledge in many domains, and simply overshooting the return-to-go can yield sub-optimal and sometimes catastrophic results.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="A6.I1.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span>
<div id="A6.I1.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A6.I1.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">These methods do not scale well with the horizon unlike BPO with Actions World Models. Even on relatively short horizons such as 100 time steps, the online decision transformer’s performance quickly drops when compared to its performance for 20 time steps.</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div>
<figure id="A6.F10" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2402.05290v2/odt_rtg_iqms.svg" id="A6.F10.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:329/235;" width="329" height="235"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 10: </span>Aggregate final performance of an online decision transformer on the Myriad environments, trained on 200000 environment steps. The <span id="A6.F10.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Expert RTG</span> is conditioned on the optimal return for each environment, while the <span id="A6.F10.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Overshot RTG</span> is conditioned on a return two times higher than the optimal return (10 seeds <math id="A6.F10.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pm" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>±</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pm</annotation></semantics></math> 95% C.I.).</figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
</section>
<section id="A7" class="ltx_appendix">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix G </span>Extended Related Work on Sequence Models in RL</h3>

<div id="A7.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A7.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Sequence models in RL have primarily been used in one of three ways. First, sequence models can be used as history encoders in RL algorithms to maximize returns in partially observable MDPs (POMDPs) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hausknecht &amp; Stone, 2015</a>; <a href="#bib.bib35" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ni et al., 2021</a>)</cite>, sometimes through a history-dependent world model <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hafner et al., 2022</a>; <a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hafner et al., 2023</a>)</cite>. Second, sequence models have recently shown promise in an imitation learning or offline reinforcement learning setting by treating MDPs as a sequence modeling problem <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chen et al., 2021</a>; <a href="#bib.bib57" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zheng et al., 2022</a>; <a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">Janner et al., 2021</a>)</cite>, usually conditioning on returns to derive desired policies. Lastly, a separate line of work has used sequence models to reshape the reward landscape for improved temporal credit assignment <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib24" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hung et al., 2019</a>; <a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">Arjona-Medina et al., 2019</a>; <a href="#bib.bib30" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liu et al., 2019</a>)</cite>. In contrast to all of these, our framework is the only one to use an <span id="A7.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">action-only</span> conditioned sequence model to directly improve long-term policy gradients in MDPs with no intermediate step. Below, we go into a detailed comparison with each area.</p>
</div>
<div id="A7.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A7.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A7.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Comparison with history-conditioned RL methods for POMDPs.</span>
History-conditioned encoders, modeled as sequence models, are often used in POMDPs in both model-free <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hausknecht &amp; Stone, 2015</a>; <a href="#bib.bib35" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ni et al., 2021</a>)</cite> and model-based methods <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hafner et al., 2022</a>; <a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hafner et al., 2023</a>)</cite>. The latter is typically also concerned with predicting observations, they are conditioned on entire history information, while our method includes only actions. The problem setup is also different; such methods are usually concerned with memory in POMDPs <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib36" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ni et al., 2023</a>)</cite>, while ours seeks to improve credit assignment in MDPs.</p>
</div>
<div id="A7.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A7.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A7.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Comparison with decision and trajectory transformers. </span> Decision transformers <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chen et al., 2021</a>; <a href="#bib.bib57" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zheng et al., 2022</a>)</cite> and trajectory transformers <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">Janner et al., 2021</a>)</cite> take a more extreme approach, casting the entire reinforcement learning problem as a sequence modeling one. Conversely, we specifically draw a parallel between policy gradients and sequence models. Their sequence models are conditioned on entire trajectories, which include states, actions, rewards and returns. While trajectory transformers predict states just like our Actions World Models, both trajectory and decision transformers also predict actions. In either case, their sequence models must first be trained on an offline dataset in an imitation learning <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">Janner et al., 2021</a>)</cite>, offline RL <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chen et al., 2021</a>)</cite>, or pre-training framework <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib57" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zheng et al., 2022</a>)</cite>, while AWMs work for an online RL setting.</p>
</div>
<div id="A7.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A7.p4.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A7.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Comparison with reward reshaping methods.</span> Perhaps more relevant, prior works have already tried harnessing advanced sequence models for improved temporal credit assignment in RL <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib24" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hung et al., 2019</a>; <a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">Arjona-Medina et al., 2019</a>; <a href="#bib.bib30" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liu et al., 2019</a>)</cite>. In these cases, the predictive power of sequence models, either an LSTM <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">Arjona-Medina et al., 2019</a>)</cite> or transformer <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib24" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hung et al., 2019</a>; <a href="#bib.bib30" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liu et al., 2019</a>)</cite> are used to redistribute or augment the given reward function to produce a surrogate reward function. This surrogate reward is then used in a more traditional model-free RL algorithm. Again, we stress a fundamental difference in the inputs of the sequence models, which all include state information. Our framework also establishes a more direct path between sequence models and credit assignment, avoiding any intermediate steps like reward reshaping.</p>
</div>
<div id="A7.p5" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A7.p5.1" class="ltx_p"></p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
</article>
